3d981f304c8648250556f864871389decad98641.prompt_preview: Original question: How do Temporal, Celery and AWS Step Functions each detect a worker that dies in the middle of a task
3d981f304c8648250556f864871389decad98641.text:
I found documentation for most of this, but I could not confirm the monitoring-events details or the exact `WorkerLostError` text. My last round of searches failed with "Server tool use limit exceeded". I did not fill those gaps from memory.

**Default behaviour: early acknowledgement**
- By default the worker acknowledges the message just before it runs the task. The reason given is that a task that has already started is never executed again. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html
- The docs say the worker cannot tell whether a task is idempotent, so they recommend idempotent tasks. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html
- I found no explicit sentence saying a task is lost if its worker dies mid-run under early ack. That follows from the two points above: the message is already acknowledged, so the broker has nothing to redeliver. I am inferring this.

**Late acknowledgement (`acks_late`)**
- `acks_late` defaults to disabled. When it is enabled, the message is acknowledged after the task has executed instead of before. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html
- The docs warn that the task may be executed twice (or multiple times) if the worker crashes mid-execution. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/reference/celery.app.task.html and https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html
- `acks_on_failure_or_timeout` is deprecated. Its replacements are `acks_on_failure` and `acks_on_timeout`. All of these apply only when `acks_late` is enabled. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html
- When `task_acks_on_failure` is disabled, failed task messages are rejected without requeue. When `task_acks_on_timeout` is disabled, timed-out task messages are rejected and requeued. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html

**Child process death and `reject_on_worker_lost`**
- Even with `acks_late` enabled, the worker acknowledges the task if the process executing it abruptly exits or is signaled (for example KILL or INT). https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html
- Setting `task_reject_on_worker_lost` to true requeues the message instead. The task then runs again on the same worker or another one. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html
- The setting is disabled by default. The docs warn that enabling it can cause message loops. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html
- `worker_lost_wait` defaults to 10 seconds. It exists because a worker killed without cleanup may already have published a result. The setting controls how long Celery waits for missing results before raising a worker-lost error. The snippet I saw was cut off, so I did not see the exact exception name in the docs. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html
- A GitHub issue (Celery 4.1.0, AMQP broker) reports that with `acks_late=True` and `reject_on_worker_lost=True`, a task was rescheduled and re-run after the worker was killed. However, `AsyncResult.get()` on the original result raised `WorkerLostError`. https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/4229
- That is a user report, not official documentation. The issue's own steps say the task ran without an exception once the worker was restarted, so the report is inconsistent on that point. I would treat the `get()` behaviour as unconfirmed.

**Visibility timeout (Redis, and similar brokers)**
- The visibility timeout is the number of seconds to wait for the worker to acknowledge a task before the message is redelivered to another worker. The Redis default is 1 hour. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/getting-started/backends-and-brokers/redis.html
- Redis has no native acknowledgement, so the transport emulates it. A received message is moved into an "unacked" hash, and its receive time is recorded in a sorted set. A periodic sweep pushes entries older than the visibility timeout back onto the queue. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/getting-started/backends-and-brokers/redis.html
- Tasks with ETA, countdown or retry delays longer than the visibility timeout get executed again, and can loop. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/getting-started/backends-and-brokers/redis.html
- Celery redeliver messages at worker shutdown. A long visibility timeout therefore only delays redelivery of "lost" tasks after a power failure or forced kill. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/getting-started/backends-and-brokers/redis.html
- Since Celery 3.0, unacknowledged Redis messages are redelivered either when the connection is closed or when the visibility timeout is exceeded. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v5.5.1/history/whatsnew-3.0.html

**Worker heartbeats and events**
- The worker's `Heart` component sends `worker-heartbeat` event messages at a regular interval. The default is 2 seconds. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/internals/reference/celery.worker.heartbeat.html
- The docs say this heartbeat is not the same as AMQP protocol-level heartbeats. https://celery-safwan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/celery.worker.consumer.html
- The worker has `--without-heartbeat` and `--heartbeat-interval` options. `--without-gossip` stops it subscribing to other workers' events. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v4.2.0/reference/celery.bin.worker.html
- The `Gossip` bootstep consumes events from other workers. https://celery-safwan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/celery.worker.consumer.html
- Task events (the `-E` flag) are optional and go to monitors such as `celery events`. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v4.2.0/reference/celery.bin.worker.html

**Not established**
- I did not confirm how long a monitor waits before treating a worker as offline when heartbeats stop.
- I did not confirm that heartbeats and events are monitoring-only and never trigger recovery of a task. The sources I saw describe recovery only through broker redelivery, visibility timeout and `reject_on_worker_lost`.
- I did not confirm the detail of how the main worker process notices that a pool child died (billiard). I also did not confirm the exact `WorkerLostError` message text.
- I did not retrieve the docs on broker connection loss. For Redis, the 3.0 release notes above say unacked messages are redelivered when the connection closes.
- I did not retrieve the docs on `task.retry` or the FAQ "Should I use retry or acks_late?". I only saw the FAQ referenced from the configuration page. Retries therefore need no further statement here, since they apply to exceptions raised inside a running task, not to a dead worker.

3fb2a75d0e1e97b5d303b420a8eccaa720266193.prompt_preview: Original question: How do Temporal, Celery and AWS Step Functions each detect a worker that dies in the middle of a task
3fb2a75d0e1e97b5d303b420a8eccaa720266193.text:
**Short answer:** None of the three has a real "is this worker alive?" probe for a task in flight. Temporal and Step Functions infer a dead worker from timeouts and missed heartbeats, and both can retry the work automatically. Celery detects a dead child process locally, and detects a lost node only through broker acknowledgement and redelivery rules. By default Celery does not re-run a task whose worker died.

## Temporal

**Detection**
- The server does not notice a crash directly. A task can be lost in delivery, or the worker can crash after calling the activity function. The service relies on the Start-To-Close timeout (https://docs.temporal.io/activity-execution).
- Every activity needs a Start-To-Close or Schedule-To-Close timeout, because the service cannot tell when a worker crashes or loses contact (https://docs.temporal.io/evaluate/features/timeouts-and-retries).
- Long-running activities should heartbeat and set a Heartbeat Timeout, which detects a lost worker sooner than a long Start-To-Close (https://docs.temporal.io/evaluate/features/timeouts-and-retries). A heartbeat is a ping from the worker to the service saying the activity is progressing and the worker has not crashed (https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection).
- Schedule-To-Start covers "no workers available or keeping up", not a mid-execution crash. It never triggers a retry (https://docs.temporal.io/evaluate/features/timeouts-and-retries).

**Recovery of activities**
- When Start-To-Close fires, the server records `ActivityTaskTimedOut`, re-adds the task to the task queue under the Retry Policy, and increments the attempt count (https://temporal.io/blog/activity-timeouts).
- Because the task returns to the shared queue, it is retried on a different worker, according to a Temporal developer. Retries continue until Schedule-To-Close, after which an `ActivityFailure` reaches the workflow code. Maximum attempts of 1 disables retries (https://community.temporal.io/t/workflow-and-activity-timeout/4745).
- An activity failure never fails the workflow unless the workflow code does so deliberately (https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection).

**Recovery of workflow code**
- If a worker dies during a workflow task, the Workflow Task Timeout (default 10 s) elapses. The service records `WorkflowTaskTimedOut` and schedules a new task. A new worker fetches the Event History and replays the workflow code to restore state (https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/event-history/event-history-java).
- Sticky queues speed up the normal case. If a worker does not start a task from its sticky queue within 5 s by default, the service reschedules it on the shared queue (https://github.com/temporalio/sdk-rust/blob/main/arch_docs/sticky_queues.md, https://docs.temporal.io/sticky-execution). A longer sticky timeout means slower failover from a dead worker (https://community.temporal.io/t/workflowtasktimedout/6932).

**Not verified:** the default Heartbeat Timeout (probably unset, so heartbeating is optional) and the default retry policy values. The researcher believed these are 1 s initial interval, 2.0 backoff and unlimited attempts, but no source confirmed it.

## Celery

**Detection**
- With the prefork pool, the parent process monitors its children. If a child is killed (for example by an OOM SIGKILL), the parent marks the task failed with `WorkerLostError('Worker exited prematurely: signal 9 (SIGKILL).')` (https://github.com/celery/billiard/issues/380, https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/5690). It then spawns a replacement child. The container keeps running, so Kubernetes reports nothing (https://engineering.backmarket.com/a-story-of-kubernetes-celery-resource-and-a-rabbit-ec2ef9e37e9f).
- `worker_lost_wait` sets how long to wait for a result that may already have been published before raising `WorkerLostError` (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html).
- For loss of a whole worker or node, detection happens at the broker: unacknowledged messages are redelivered when the connection closes or the visibility timeout is exceeded (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v5.5.1/history/whatsnew-3.0.html). I could not retrieve sources on `broker_heartbeat` or RabbitMQ dead-consumer detection, so the connection-closed claim rests only on that 3.0 page.

**Recovery**
- **Default (`acks_late=False`):** the message is acknowledged just before the task runs (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/reference/celery.app.task.html). So the broker has already discarded it, and the task is not re-run. It shows as failed with `WorkerLostError`. This is inferred from that doc and the issue logs, not stated in one sentence.
- **`acks_late=True`:** the message is acknowledged after the task runs, and the docs warn the task may execute twice if the worker crashes mid-execution (same page). Even so, the worker acknowledges the task if the child process abruptly exits or is signaled. To get redelivery in that case, enable `task_reject_on_worker_lost` (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html). Wolt recommends combining the two settings (https://careers.wolt.com/en/blog/tech/5-tips-for-writing-production-ready-celery-tasks).
- **Caveats:** a user reports that with this setting, `AsyncResult.get()` still raises `WorkerLostError` even though the task is rescheduled (https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/4229). A recent PR describes an edge case where a child dies after the task succeeded, and the task is requeued and runs again (https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/10752).
- **Visibility timeout (Redis):** a task not acknowledged within the timeout is redelivered to another worker. The default is 1 hour (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/getting-started/backends-and-brokers/redis.html). A task running longer than the timeout can be picked up by a second worker while the first is still running it (https://dev.to/artemooon/celery-redis-at-scale-designing-a-reliable-and-efficient-task-queue-in-production-27nh).

**Not established:** the current default of `task_reject_on_worker_lost` (docs show `None`, read as off). Retries (`autoretry_for`, `task.retry`) were not covered. My inference is that they apply only to exceptions raised inside the task, not to a lost worker.

## AWS Step Functions

**Detection**
- Step Functions has no worker health check. It uses timeouts and heartbeats. A task waits for a success or failure response within `TimeoutSeconds`, and if none arrives the task fails (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html).
- `HeartbeatSeconds` must be a positive integer smaller than `TimeoutSeconds`. If more time than that passes between heartbeats, the state fails with `States.Timeout` (same page). Workers send heartbeats with `SendTaskHeartbeat` using the task token (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSJavaSDK/latest/javadoc/com/amazonaws/services/stepfunctions/AWSStepFunctionsClient.html).
- The default for both timeouts is 99,999,999 seconds. Without an explicit timeout, a task can wait indefinitely for a response that never comes (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/sfn-best-practices.html). For callback (`.waitForTaskToken`) tasks, AWS recommends adding `HeartbeatSeconds` (same page).

**Recovery**
- `Retry` is a list of retriers with `ErrorEquals`, `IntervalSeconds`, `MaxAttempts` and `BackoffRate`. Defaults reported by secondary sources are 1 s, 3 attempts and 2.0 (https://dev.to/dashbird/aws-step-functions-error-handling-49d0, https://dashbird.io/blog/aws-step-functions-error-handling/). I did not retrieve the official AWS page for these.
- Timeouts can be retried, for example a `States.Timeout` retrier with `MaxAttempts: 2` (https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-12-handle-errors-retries-step-functions/view). Retriers are evaluated in order, so specific ones go before `States.ALL`.
- Once retries are exhausted, `Catch` routes to a fallback state, optionally using `ResultPath` to attach the error (same oneuptime source). A timeout catch often leads to a `Fail` state or a compensation step (https://dev.to/aws-builders/mastering-aws-step-functions-error-handling-j39).
- For Activities, a retry plausibly makes a new task available to the next `GetActivityTask` poll, so another worker can take it. This is my inference, not something I found stated.

**Not verified:** `MaxDelaySeconds`, `JitterStrategy`, and billing treatment of retries.

## Comparison

| | Temporal | Celery | Step Functions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Detection | Timeouts, plus optional activity heartbeats. The service cannot see a crash directly. | Parent notices a dead child immediately. Node loss is detected via the broker connection and visibility timeout. | `TimeoutSeconds` and optional `HeartbeatSeconds` |
| Default if no timeout is set | Start-To-Close or Schedule-To-Close is required | Not applicable. Redis visibility timeout is 1 h. | 99,999,999 s, so effectively waits forever |
| Automatic re-run by default | Yes, under the Retry Policy | No. The task fails with `WorkerLostError` unless `acks_late` and `reject_on_worker_lost` are set. | No. Retry or Catch must be configured. |
| Workflow or orchestration state | Rebuilt by replay on another worker | None. Celery has no central tracker of tasks in flight (my inference). | The state machine is managed by the service |

**Guarantees and idempotency:** all three give at-least-once behaviour once recovery is on, so tasks should be idempotent.
- **Temporal:** a timed-out activity may already have partly run before it is retried.
- **Celery:** the docs explicitly warn of double execution with `acks_late`. Duplicates can also come from the visibility timeout or the post-success edge case.
- **Step Functions:** a timed-out worker may still be running when a retry hands the work to another one. This follows from the timeout design rather than a source I retrieved.

3feb1cc48252ce4897aa4fe8630af48dc4cb90af.prompt_preview: Original question: What are the known limits of Concord's duplicate detection and tracing according to its documentation
3feb1cc48252ce4897aa4fe8630af48dc4cb90af.text:
**How duplicate detection works**

- The supervisor checks each subgoal before dispatch and reuses the output of an earlier duplicate, defined as the same normalized text and same inputs, or embedding similarity above a threshold. [README.md § What works today]
- In a supervised run a subgoal moves `pending → checking → ready → leased → done`, so a duplicate is caught before any worker spends tokens on it. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- The design is "normalized key plus embedding similarity", because repeated subgoals usually arrive reworded. Inputs are part of the comparison: the same instruction applied to different inputs is different work. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- Each pre-dispatch check gets its own span in the trace. A duplicate served from an earlier result links to the span that produced that result. [README.md § What works today; tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgoal graph]
- Measured result: exact duplicates caught 8/8 (100%), against a 100% target. With the supervisor, the duplicate never reaches a worker. Without it, the result is correct but the work is done twice. Tokens saved on runs with an exact duplicate: 11.2%. [README.md § Scorecard]
- False alarms on healthy runs: 0/16. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Figures come from 72 scripted runs on a mock model, so token figures are word counts and only the relative difference means anything. [README.md § Scorecard]

**Limits of duplicate detection**

1. **Reworded duplicates are not caught by default.**
   - Reworded duplicate catch rate is 0/16 (0%), against a target of ≥ 90%. [README.md § Scorecard]
   - Similarity matching is off unless an embedder is supplied. [README.md § Scorecard]
   - Documentation on removal: a real embedding model must be plugged in. It is planned for the real-model phase. [README.md § Scorecard; README.md § What works today]
   - The gap is described as visible and left in on purpose. [README.md § Scorecard]

2. **The built-in word-overlap embedder does not catch true paraphrases.**
   - With it switched on, light edits are caught (7/8 in the harness, 38/40 in a larger run). True paraphrases are not caught (0/40). It catches reordered or lightly edited subgoals only. [README.md § Scorecard; README.md § What works today]
   - It ships for tests. [README.md § What works today]
   - Documentation on removal: true paraphrases need a real embedding model, planned for the real-model phase. [README.md § What works today]

3. **The word-overlap embedder can reuse the wrong output.**
   - In the larger run it reused the wrong output once in 40 look-alike runs, where two subgoals differed only in their topic. Word overlap cannot tell which word changed. [README.md § Scorecard]
   - This is the stated reason similarity stays off until a real embedding model is plugged in. [README.md § Scorecard]
   - Documentation on removal: a real embedding model. The documents do not say whether a real model would fully eliminate this failure. [README.md § Scorecard]

**Limits of tracing (as it relates to duplicates and structure)**

4. **Attempts are deliberately not nested under their dependencies.**
   - Every attempt is a direct child of the run's root span and carries span links to the spans that finished its dependencies. [tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgraph]
   - Reason: a dependency's span has already ended when the dependent starts, and trace viewers treat a child starting after its parent ended as clock skew. Jaeger shifted such spans by up to 86ms and attached warnings when an earlier version nested them. [tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgoal graph]
   - This is a design choice, not a stated gap. The documents give no fix because none is described as needed.

**Related gaps in the same area**

5. **Off-task output is not caught at all.** The score is 0/8 with and without the supervisor, and there is no drift check yet. The drift check is a later phase. The roadmap says it will be a yes/no rubric tuned on a labelled set. [README.md § Scorecard; ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]

6. **Recovery after a crash is not built.** "Finished subgoals re-run after a crash" is not measured. [README.md § Scorecard]

**Not covered by the passages**

- Beyond the scorecard rows above, the passages do not describe limits of normalization itself, the similarity threshold value, or how duplicates behave across runs.
- They do not describe tracing limits beyond the nesting decision, and say nothing about what real-model embedding would need in terms of work, other than that it is planned.
- No passage from docs/tracing.md beyond the one section was provided.

411aaf78e132da67c33605a36eeffd4acaee277c.text:
I could only answer part of this. My search tool hit its usage limit after one successful search, so I found nothing on recent LLM multi-agent papers. I won't guess at paper titles or claims from memory.

**Origin (supported by a source)**
- The first blackboard system was the HEARSAY-II speech-understanding system, which evolved between 1971 and 1976 (Erman et al., 1980). [https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1609/aimag.v7i2.537]
- The source for this is Nii's AI Magazine article "The Blackboard Model of Problem Solving and the Evolution of Blackboard Architectures". It says many later systems have a similar organization and run-time behavior. [https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1609/aimag.v7i2.537]
- The reference list for that article names Erman, Hayes-Roth, Lesser and Reddy as the HEARSAY-II authors. [https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1609/aimag.v7i2.537]
- The page I retrieved gave only the abstract and references, not a full definition. I'm not quoting the textbook account of knowledge sources, a shared blackboard and a controller, because I didn't verify it here.

**Recent LLM multi-agent papers: not found**
- I have no verified sources on how recent LLM multi-agent papers use the blackboard pattern. To check this, search arXiv for "blackboard" together with "LLM multi-agent". I can retry if you ask again.

**How your own project, Concord, uses it (from your documents)**
- In Concord, the blackboard is the shared state that planner, workers and supervisor coordinate through. [README.md § Concord]
- Subgoal records live in Redis. Every state change is an atomic Lua script that also appends an event to a Redis Stream. [README.md § What works today]
- A subgoal is released when all its dependencies are done. [README.md § What works today]
- The supervisor reads the event stream through a consumer group, so it resumes after a restart. [README.md § What works today]
- Concord's status is early development. The planner, specialists and Claude client have not been run against the real API. [README.md § Concord]

420c7ae26a475ce2c48ddf9a555845fb401499d4.prompt_preview: Original question: What delivery guarantees do Redis Pub/Sub, Redis Streams with consumer groups, and Apache Kafka consu
420c7ae26a475ce2c48ddf9a555845fb401499d4.text:
**Short answer:** Redis Streams with consumer groups is the lightest option of the three that does not lose messages across a consumer restart, provided persistence is configured. Pub/Sub loses messages. Kafka also avoids loss, but it is heavier. The Streams and Kafka claims below are mostly not verified against official documentation, so check them before relying on them.

**Redis Pub/Sub: at-most-once, loses messages across a restart (sourced)**
- The official docs describe delivery as "once if at all". If the subscriber hits an error or a network disconnect, the message is "forever lost" (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/pubsub/).
- Messages go only to clients subscribed at publish time. A subscriber that is offline when a message is published misses it, and Redis's guide advises keeping durable state in keys or a Stream (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/pub-sub/dotnet/).
- It follows that a restarting consumer misses everything published while it was down. The official page does not literally say "no replay". That is an inference from the wording above.
- The Redis docs point to Streams for stronger guarantees. They say stream messages are persisted and support at-most-once and at-least-once delivery (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/pubsub/).

**Redis Streams with consumer groups: at-least-once, with caveats (mostly unverified)**
- Confirmed: a stream is an append-only log. Producers append with XADD, and consumers in a group read with XREADGROUP (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/streaming/redis-py/).
- The details below come from background knowledge and were not checked against the official pages:
  - Delivered but unacknowledged entries stay in the group's pending entries list (PEL), tied to a consumer name.
  - Reading with `>` returns only never-delivered entries. Reading with `0` returns the consumer's own pending entries, so a restarted consumer can re-process them.
  - XACK removes an entry from the PEL.
  - XCLAIM and XAUTOCLAIM let another consumer take over entries that have sat idle too long.
  - Together these give at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are possible.
- Durability depends on configuration, also unverified:
  - RDB snapshots can lose recent writes.
  - AOF with `appendfsync everysec` can lose about a second of writes. `always` is safest but slowest.
  - Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose acknowledged writes. WAIT reduces that risk but does not eliminate it.
- Pages to check: https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/, https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/persistence/, https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/replication/

**Kafka consumer groups: at-least-once if you commit after processing (not verified from Kafka's docs)**
- The only sourced point is from a client library's docs, not Kafka's own. The default auto-commit can lose data on a critical failure, so set `enable_auto_commit=False` and commit manually after processing (https://aiokafka.readthedocs.io/en/stable/examples/manual_commit.html).
- Background knowledge, unverified:
  - Offsets are stored in the internal `__consumer_offsets` topic, and a restarted consumer resumes from its committed offset.
  - Committing after processing gives at-least-once delivery. Committing before gives at-most-once.
  - Exactly-once needs transactions and `read_committed`, and applies to Kafka-to-Kafka flows.
  - Retention limits on offsets and logs matter, and `auto.offset.reset` governs what happens when no committed offset exists.
- I could not retrieve the official Kafka pages ("Message Delivery Semantics", the consumer configs, and the KRaft operations section).

**Which is lightest without losing messages**
- If you already run Redis, use Streams with consumer groups. It needs no new infrastructure, and a restarted consumer can recover its pending entries.
- For the guarantee to hold, enable AOF persistence (`everysec` or `always`) and acknowledge only after processing succeeds.
- Make processing idempotent, for example by deduplicating on the stream entry ID. Redelivery after a crash between processing and XACK is expected under at-least-once.
- Kafka becomes justified when you need very high throughput, long-term retention and replay, many independent consumer groups, or replicated durability without Redis's asynchronous-replication gap. That comparison is my own judgment, since the operational weight of Kafka was not sourced. Kafka also means running brokers and managing partitions.

42980ce546c69b18e80022d62e41fbdf643f61dd.prompt_preview: Original question: What are the practical differences between BM25 and dense embedding retrieval for a small document se
42980ce546c69b18e80022d62e41fbdf643f61dd.text:
I could only get partial coverage. The search tool hit its usage limit partway through, so several topics were not searched. Everything below comes from snippets I actually saw.

**Established**

- BEIR, a zero-shot benchmark, reports that BM25 trails neural retrievers by 7–18 points on in-domain MS MARCO. The same paper says BEIR shows BM25 to be a strong baseline for generalization to new domains. This supports the point about domain shift: dense models trained on one distribution do not reliably transfer. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.08663
- Chunking has a strong, often non-linear effect on dense retrieval, according to a 2026 chunking study. It describes the trade-off this way:
  - Smaller chunks favour precise matching but risk losing context.
  - Larger chunks capture broader semantics, but with more redundancy and query mismatch. https://arxiv.org/html/2603.06976
- The same study benchmarked 36 chunking methods across six domains and five embedding models. It reports consistent performance hierarchies across domains and models. It also reports that the best chunking approach depends on the domain, and that even the smallest model benefits from the domain-preferred segmentation. Larger embedding models score higher in absolute terms under every chunking strategy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06976 and https://www.researchgate.net/publication/401721135_A_Systematic_Investigation_of_Document_Chunking_Strategies_and_Embedding_Sensitivity
- A separate IT-RAG-Bench ablation found that nDCG@10 reached at least 95% of its peak by a chunk size of 32 tokens. The authors attribute that to the corpus, whose passages average about 60 tokens, so the result is corpus-specific. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.23618
- The same paper has a latency and cost table. It lists an API embedding model (GE2) with median query latency of about 232 ms and a published price of $0.025 per 1M tokens. It lists BGE-M3, a model that can be self-hosted, with a median of about 31 ms. This shows that API and local models differ in cost model and latency. I did not see the full table, so I cannot report other rows. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.23618
- A third paper describes the standard dense pipeline. Documents are split into overlapping chunks because of embedding input-length limits. Chunk and query embeddings are normalized, and relevance is cosine similarity. The chunk size, overlap and embedding model are all tunable choices that change results. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.30846

**Not established (no source retrieved)**

- Failures on exact terms, identifiers and rare entities. I did not find a source such as the entity-questions work on DPR vs BM25.
- Paraphrase and semantic matching strengths, other than the general contrast that lexical retrieval relies on exact term matching. That contrast comes from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.30846.
- Cross-lingual and multilingual retrieval. BGE-M3 appears only in the cost table, not as evidence of multilingual performance.
- Any evidence specific to small collections, and compute or embedding cost beyond the one price and latency row above.

4418645fdf71c337b6bbe39658a057aa7cf7c7cf.prompt_preview: Question: What span names and attributes do the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define for agent invocations, m
4418645fdf71c337b6bbe39658a057aa7cf7c7cf.text:
**Short answer:** Every `gen_ai.*` span and attribute is still at **Development** status. The conventions now live in a separate repo, `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai`. I could confirm the model-call details and the stability status from primary sources. I could not confirm the exact span name and kind for `invoke_agent` and `execute_tool` before my search quota ran out, so those rest on secondary sources.

**Stability**
- The inference (model call) section of the spec is marked "Status: Development" [https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md].
- The operation-name values `chat`, `create_agent`, `embeddings` and `execute_tool` are each listed as Development [https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/registry/attributes/gen-ai/].
- The agent-span attributes (such as `gen_ai.agent.name`) are Development, while `error.type` is Stable. `error.type` comes from the core conventions [https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md].
- The conventions moved out of the main repo. The semantic-conventions release notes say all gen_ai.* attributes, metrics, events and spans were deprecated and moved to the dedicated GenAI repository [https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/releases].
- On releases, one GitHub issue says the new repo "has no release yet" [https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/4140]. That is a secondary source. I did not check the repo's tags myself.

**Model calls (inference), from the primary spec**
- Span name: {gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}, for example `chat gpt-4` [https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md].
- Kind: SHOULD be CLIENT, and MAY be INTERNAL for models running in the same process [same URL].
- Attributes that should be set when the span is created: `gen_ai.operation.name`, `gen_ai.provider.name`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `server.address` and `server.port` [same URL].
- Token usage is recorded as `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`. This comes from a GitHub issue and a blog post, not the spec text I retrieved [https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/4140].

**Agent invocations and tool calls**

4a16873e902214eb82e338fc37cd722602cd86b4.prompt_preview: Original question: What are the practical differences between BM25 and dense embedding retrieval for a small document se
4a16873e902214eb82e338fc37cd722602cd86b4.text:
I could not run the BEIR-specific searches because the search tool hit its usage limit. The findings below come only from the first round of searches. I have no direct BEIR numbers and no small-corpus evidence from a primary source.

**Established by the searches**

- Bruch et al. (TOIS 2023) studied hybrid search as a fusion of lexical and semantic scores. They compared a convex combination (a weighted sum) with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). They report that RRF is sensitive to its parameters, and that learning a convex combination is generally agnostic to the choice of score normalization. The abstract is cut off, but it goes on to say that a convex combination outperforms RRF in in-domain and out-of-domain settings. Sources: https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3596512 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.11934
- The Bruch paper describes the argument for RRF. An earlier study argued RRF may suit better because it is non-parametric and can be used zero-shot, and it showed strong zero-shot results on several benchmark datasets. The two positions therefore conflict. Source: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3596512
- A third-party GitHub issue quotes the Bruch result as +1.5 to +3.2 nDCG points over RRF on 9 of 9 datasets. That is a secondary summary, not the paper itself. Source: https://github.com/daniel-ospina/tortoise/issues/4210
- The same issue says the author's own in-house tests found equal-weight RRF cost about 2 nDCG points, and they kept a weighted RRF that favours the vector side. This is anecdotal evidence that fusion weights matter. Source: https://github.com/daniel-ospina/tortoise/issues/4210
- A 2026 arXiv benchmark on text-and-table documents (TAT-DQA and other subsets) found that RRF hybrid retrieval improves over both BM25 and dense alone across all metrics and all dataset subsets. The largest gain was on TAT-DQA, +8.1 points Recall@5 over BM25. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01733v1
- The same paper reports that a two-stage pipeline of hybrid retrieval plus neural reranking reached Recall@5 of 0.816 and MRR@3 of 0.605, beating all single-stage methods. It uses RRF with k = 60. Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.01733
- That paper's related-work section says hybrid retrieval consistently improves recall by 15–30% over single-method pipelines. This is a literature claim that cites another source, so treat it as weakly supported. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2604.01733v1
- Query types where hybrid helps, per a vendor blog: use hybrid when queries mix exact identifiers (error codes, product names, API endpoints, legal terms) with natural-language intent. The same snippet says pure vector search suits queries that are entirely semantic when the embedding model is already strong. The snippet was truncated, so this is the author's guidance, not measured evidence. Source: https://www.premai.io/blog/hybrid-search-for-rag-bm25-splade-and-vector-search-combined/
- A small teaching repo with a 12-document corpus and 8 queries reports that BM25 wins on exact terms, IDs and jargon, and dense wins on paraphrases and concepts. It also says that cross-encoder reranking of the top-k is the cheapest relevance boost. It is a toy demonstration, not a rigorous benchmark. Source: https://github.com/chandrahas748812-cmyk/hybrid-search-lab
- On Banglish social-media retrieval, a BM25 plus Sentence Transformer RRF hybrid placed 6th in a shared task, with MAP 0.123 and NDCG 0.376. That is weak evidence for hybrid, because it did not win. Source: https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-4173/T3-7.pdf
- Complexity: Elastic's blog describes two implementations, RRF and weighted sum of scores. It applies them to combining BM25 with Elastic's learned sparse encoder (ELSER), not with dense embeddings. Source: https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/improving-information-retrieval-elastic-stack-hybrid
- Implementation guidance from the repos and blogs: the two retrievers run in parallel on every query, a fusion step merges the results, and an optional cross-encoder reranks the top candidates. Weighted sums need score normalization (e.g. min-max). RRF needs only ranks and a constant k (60 is the common default). Sources: https://github.com/RishDevs/hybrid-search-engine and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.01733

**Not established**

- I have no BEIR per-dataset numbers for BM25, dense and hybrid, and I did not retrieve the original BEIR paper. From memory only, and unverified here, BEIR's finding was that BM25 is a strong zero-shot baseline and dense models often underperform it out of domain.
- I found no source that tests hybrid gains specifically on small corpora (hundreds to thousands of documents). The only small-corpus evidence is the 12-document toy repo. The writer should say this is an open gap and not claim that the gains hold for small corpora.
- I found no rigorous source on query types where hybrid does not help. The only hint is the vendor claim that purely semantic queries with a strong embedder may not need it.
- I found no measurements of latency or infrastructure cost for hybrid versus single-method retrieval.

52ea5e045ca9e6ca3aab87d6b7de1fb294256844.prompt_preview: Original question: How do Temporal, Restate and DBOS each implement durable execution, and what does each require of the
52ea5e045ca9e6ca3aab87d6b7de1fb294256844.text:
Results are strings; parse.I could not run the last round of searches (determinism and journal-mismatch errors, awakeables and durable promises, `ctx.run` retry semantics) because the search tool hit its usage limit. The findings below come from the first four searches. Items I could not confirm are listed at the end.

**How Restate implements durable execution**
- Restate is a server, plus a thin SDK in your service. It acts as a message broker or reverse proxy in front of your services. Your workflows and business logic are service handlers that use the SDK. https://docs.restate.dev/tour/workflows
- Handlers are durable functions that can be invoked over HTTP, Kafka, or typed clients. https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/handlers
- The server keeps a bidirectional connection to the running handler. Through the SDK, the code can journal steps, send events to other handlers, read and write state, and create persistent futures (callbacks) and timers. https://restate.dev/blog/building-a-modern-durable-execution-engine-from-first-principles
- The server's view of an invocation and its journal is the ground truth. Function executions may be cancelled, reset or retried as needed. https://restate.dev/blog/building-a-modern-durable-execution-engine-from-first-principles
- Every external interaction is recorded to a persistent log before the application observes its result. If the process crashes, the engine restarts the function and replays the journal. Completed steps return their recorded results instantly, until execution catches up to the failure point. https://restate.dev/what-is-durable-execution
- Internally, the architecture is partitioned and log-centric:
  - Ingress identifies the target handler and partition from the workflow ID, virtual-object key or idempotency key. It forwards the call to the partition's current leader.
  - The durable log is called "Bifrost". Each partition has one sequencer/leader, and a write commits when a quorum of replicas acknowledges it.
  - Each partition has a processor that tails the log and invokes your handler code over a bidirectional stream. It keeps a materialized cache in embedded RocksDB. The cache holds journals, idempotency metadata, per-key virtual-object state and timers.
  - Processor state is periodically snapshotted to S3 for bounded recovery.
  - https://docs.restate.dev/references/architecture
- Snapshots allow the log to be trimmed. Without them, a new partition processor would need to replay the whole partition log. https://docs.restate.dev/server/snapshots

**Service types**
- Basic Service: stateless handlers with unlimited parallelism.
- Virtual Object: keyed, with isolated K/V state and a single writer per key, plus concurrent readers.
- Workflow: a `run` handler that executes exactly once per ID, plus concurrent shared handlers. Workflows also have "workflow promises".
- https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/services
- The context type depends on the service type: `Context`, `ObjectContext`, `ObjectSharedContext`, `WorkflowContext` or `WorkflowSharedContext`. Exclusive handlers can read and write state, and only one runs per key at a time. Shared handlers can only read state and run concurrently. https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/handlers
- Handler input and output can be any JSON-serializable type. https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/handlers

**What Restate requires of developer code**
- Handlers receive a Restate `ctx` and use it for durable actions. The example is `ctx.run("process", () => ...)`. https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/handlers
- Every external call is wrapped in `ctx.run(...)` so the engine can journal it. https://restate.dev/what-is-durable-execution
- `run` actions persist non-deterministic operations such as database writes or external API calls. https://docs.restate.dev/tour/workflows
- Agent LLM calls and tool executions are wrapped in `ctx.run()`. https://docs.restate.dev/ai/patterns/durable-agents
- State is accessed through the context (`ctx.get` and `ctx.set` in a virtual object). https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/services
- Calls to other services go through the context, for example `ctx.serviceClient(...)`. https://docs.restate.dev/tour/workflows
- Saga compensations are written by the developer in code, using `ctx.run`. https://docs.restate.dev/tour/workflows
- Code is deployed as a normal HTTP endpoint (a "deployment") and registered with the server. https://docs.restate.dev/services/versioning

**Versioning**
- Restate uses immutable deployments. Each code version gets its own unique endpoint and is registered with Restate. Restate sends retries to the same endpoint the request started on. New requests go to the latest version, and in-flight invocations stay on their original one. https://docs.restate.dev/services/versioning and https://restate.dev/blog/dealing-with-versioning-in-long-running-agents
- Registering the same URI again is an error (META0004). It can be forced, but that can leave in-flight invocations in an unrecoverable state. https://docs.restate.dev/references/errors
- `--force` re-registration is acceptable only in local development. https://docs.restate.dev/services/versioning
- Long-running handlers (days or months) force you to keep old deployments around. The docs recommend breaking work into smaller chunks with delayed calls. https://docs.restate.dev/services/versioning
- FaaS platforms (Lambda versions, Vercel commit URLs and others) give immutable versions automatically. https://docs.restate.dev/services/versioning

**Not confirmed from sources (searches did not complete)**
- I have no source for the determinism rules. That covers the SDK's deterministic helpers (random numbers, time, UUIDs) and what happens when replay diverges from the journal. Restate does require handler code to be deterministic outside `ctx.run`. The pages I read imply this, because they say non-deterministic operations must go in `run`, but none states the rule or the mismatch error.
- I have no source for durable promises in the sense of awakeables or `ctx.promise`. The only mention found was that workflows have "workflow promises".
- I have no source for the retry behaviour of `ctx.run`, such as at-least-once semantics or retry policies.

5403818bcf29c46bbf0d3055bc1f351b622ffbbe.prompt_preview: Question: What is a fencing token in distributed locking, why do lease-based locks need one, and how do etcd and ZooKeep
5403818bcf29c46bbf0d3055bc1f351b622ffbbe.text:
**A fencing token is a number that the lock service increases every time a client acquires the lock. The client sends it with every write, and the storage layer rejects any write carrying an older token than one it has already seen.**

**What it is.** Kleppmann describes it as a number that increases each time a client acquires the lock, and says it must be included with every write request to the storage service. He also notes that this requires the storage server to take an active role: it must reject any write whose token has gone backwards. (Source: https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html)

**Why lease-based locks need one.** A lease expires on a timer, so the holder can lose the lock without knowing it. Typical causes are a GC pause, a stalled process or a slow network. When it resumes it still believes it holds the lock and writes, while a new holder is already working. The lock check on the client side cannot close this gap. Only the resource can, by comparing tokens. Kleppmann's example shows this: client 1 gets token 33, then pauses. Its lease expires and client 2 gets a higher token. The storage server then rejects client 1's late write. I'm paraphrasing the example from the article's snippet, which was cut off in my results. Kleppmann's article cited by Jepsen makes the same point. Jepsen says that without a lock-service token you must rely on the storage system's own transactional correctness. If the lock service provides a token, it is included with every operation so that no earlier holder's operations interleave with the current holder's. (https://jepsen.io/analyses/etcd-3.4.3) Secondary sources say Redlock produces no such monotonic token, which is a main criticism of it (e.g. https://medium.com/towardsdev/implementing-distributed-locks-correctly-5a35179422a6). I did not check Redis's own documentation on this.

**etcd.** Jepsen's analysis says you can use the revision of the lock key as a globally ordered fencing token. (https://jepsen.io/analyses/etcd-3.4.3.pdf) The lock key is attached to a lease. etcd's own lock API docs, quoted by Jepsen, say the key can be used with transactions so updates happen only while holding the lock. (https://jepsen.io/analyses/etcd-3.4.3) In practice you use the key's `mod_revision`. A third-party Go library does this: its README lists lease-based crash safety and `mod_revision` fencing tokens. (https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/ubgo/lock/etcdlock) Jepsen also points out that the etcd docs don't describe what guarantees the locks themselves give. The token only helps if the downstream store checks it. For etcd-held data, that check can be a transaction comparing revisions.

**ZooKeeper.** The official lock recipe creates a sequential, ephemeral znode. The client holds the lock if its znode has the lowest sequence number suffix. (https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/r3.1.2/recipes.html) The recipe itself doesn't mention fencing. Kleppmann says: "you can use the zxid or the znode version number as fencing token". (https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html) Note that ZooKeeper's ephemeral nodes are tied to a session timeout. That is the same lease-style expiry, so the same stale-holder problem applies.

**Caveat.** Neither system enforces the token for you. Your storage layer must remember the highest token it has seen and reject lower ones. One blog on etcd fencing makes the same point: the token works only when the downstream resource enforces it atomically. I did not verify that claim against etcd's documentation.

**Your project docs.** They don't mention fencing tokens. The README says the Redis-based workers lease subgoals and keep them alive with heartbeats. The supervisor requeues a subgoal when heartbeats stop. If a requeued worker was only slow, not dead, a late `complete` write could clash with the retry. The passages don't say whether the blackboard's Lua scripts guard against this, so I can't say whether it's handled.

58424f017069078e11309d2fbbd39efc4d9316be.prompt_preview: Original question: According to Concord's own scorecard, which failures does its supervisor catch and which does it miss
58424f017069078e11309d2fbbd39efc4d9316be.text:
**How the supervisor detects failures (design)**

What it monitors:
- It reads the blackboard's event stream through a Redis consumer group, so it resumes after a restart. [README.md § What works today]
- Redis Streams were chosen over pub/sub because pub/sub drops messages when the consumer is slow or restarting. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- Every blackboard state change is an atomic Lua script that also appends an event to the stream. [README.md § What works today]

Its checks and interventions:
- Dead worker: it requeues subgoals whose worker stopped sending heartbeats. Stall detection is based on leases and heartbeats. [README.md § What works today; ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- Pre-dispatch check: in a supervised run a subgoal moves pending → checking → ready → leased → done, so a duplicate is caught before any worker spends tokens on it. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- Duplicate reuse: it reuses the output of an earlier duplicate when the normalized text and inputs match, or when embedding similarity is above a threshold. Inputs are part of the comparison, since the same instruction on different inputs is different work. [README.md § What works today; ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- Token budget: it halts the run when it goes over its token budget. [README.md § What works today]
- Logging: every intervention is logged as a `supervisor.*` event with its reason. [README.md § What works today]
- Tracing: when a worker dies, the supervisor writes a `concord.attempt.lost` span on its behalf, because a dead worker cannot end its own span. It also writes a `concord.supervisor.requeue` child span. Each pre-dispatch check gets a `concord.supervisor.check` span. [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]

Documented limitations and known gaps:
- Reworded duplicates are not caught by default. Similarity matching is off unless an embedder is supplied. [README.md § Scorecard]
- The only shipped embedder is a word-overlap one for tests. It catches reordered or lightly edited subgoals, not true paraphrases, which need a real embedding model planned for the real-model phase. [README.md § What works today]
- With that embedder on, it caught 7/8 light edits (38/40 in a larger run) and 0/40 true paraphrases. In the larger run it reused the wrong output once in 40 look-alike runs, where subgoals differed only in topic, because word overlap cannot tell which word changed. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Off-task output is not caught at all, because there is no drift check yet; it is a later phase. [README.md § Scorecard] The planned design is a yes/no rubric tuned on a labelled set, not a raw score. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- Hung workers are not caught by the supervisor. They are caught by the worker's own deadline. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Recovery of finished subgoals after a crash is not built, so "finished subgoals re-run after a crash" is not measured. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Everything was measured on a mock model, so token figures are word counts and only relative differences mean anything. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Intended scope is 5 to 20 subgoals, parallel readers, one writer. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]

**Scorecard results these designs explain**
- Exact duplicates: 8/8 caught. Tokens saved on runs with an exact duplicate: 11.2%. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Reworded duplicates: 0/16 by default. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Dead worker: 8/8 correct with the supervisor versus 0/8 without (the run hangs), detected in about 0.4s at worst against a 0.80s target. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Supervisor restart mid-run: 8/8. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Off-task output: 0/8 caught, 0/8 correct either way. [README.md § Scorecard]
- False alarms on healthy runs: 0/16. [README.md § Scorecard]

**Not covered by the passages**
- No passage describes the exact similarity threshold, the heartbeat or lease durations beyond the scorecard's "2 × lease" target of 0.80s, or how the token budget is counted.
- No passage addresses published studies of multi-agent failure modes, so the comparison part of the question is not supported here.

5d893af472874bff97be3dc75871c8eff01d2efe.prompt_preview: Question: How does Jaeger's clock skew adjustment work, when does it change span timestamps, and how can it be turned of
5d893af472874bff97be3dc75871c8eff01d2efe.text:
**Short answer:** Jaeger's query service shifts span timestamps at read time when the causal order looks wrong. It adds a warning to each span it moves. You turn it off by setting the maximum adjustment to zero: `--query.max-clock-skew-adjustment=0s` in v1, or `max_clock_skew_adjust` in v2. I did not confirm the v2 default or the v2 YAML behaviour (details below).

**How it works**
- Spans from different hosts are combined in the backend, and clocks on those hosts drift. A server span can then appear to start before the client span that called it. The query service uses the causal relationships between spans to correct for this. [https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/]
- The adjuster changes span start times and log timestamps for spans that look "off" relative to their parent. [https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.59.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go]
- When it moves a server span inside its parent's bounds, Jaeger can't know the real split between request and response latency. It assumes they are equal and centres the child in the parent. [https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/2.22/deployment/configuration/]
- Every adjusted span gets a UI warning that states the exact delta applied. [https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/2.22/deployment/configuration/]
- The adjustment happens in the query service and UI, not in what was stored. This is my reading of the docs, which describe it as adjusting "in the UI".

**When it changes timestamps**
- It acts when a child span's timing is inconsistent with its parent's, for example a child that starts after the parent has ended.
- The flag is the maximum delta by which timestamps may be adjusted. [https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.59/cli/] That limit was added so adjustments could be capped. [https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/pull/2119]
- This matches your project's `tracing.md`. It says Jaeger shifted spans by up to 86ms and attached warnings when attempts were nested under their dependencies. It also says Jaeger will report adjustments if no root span is open. [tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgoal graph, § Limits]

**How to turn it off**
- **v1:** Set `--query.max-clock-skew-adjustment` to `0s`. The flag description says 0s disables the adjustment. [https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.59/cli/]
- **v1 default:** Since v1.20 the default is already `0s`, so it is off unless someone enabled it. [https://newreleases.io/project/github/jaegertracing/jaeger/release/v1.20.0] The reason was the issue "Clock Skew Adjuster considered harmful". [https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/pull/2513]
- **v2:** The equivalent YAML is `extensions: jaeger_query: max_clock_skew_adjust: <duration>`. [https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/6565]

**What I could not confirm**
- The v2 default value. Your traces were adjusted, so the instance you used may have a non-zero value set, or v2 may behave differently.
- Whether `0s` is honoured in v2. The v2 bug report (#6565) says a configured duration was not applied, but the snippet I retrieved was cut off. Check that issue and your Jaeger version before relying on it.
- The exact algorithm beyond the descriptions above. I did not read the adjuster source in full.

**For your project:** Turning the adjustment off only hides the symptom. The fix your docs describe is better: keep attempts as children of a real root span (`workflow_span`) and link them to their dependencies with span links instead of nesting them. [tracing.md]

5df925af78fccb767381efedfae7a7868b542b4f.prompt_preview: Original question: What is a fencing token in distributed locking, why do lease-based locks need one, and how do etcd an
5df925af78fccb767381efedfae7a7868b542b4f.text:
**Findings for my part: what a fencing token is and why lease-based locks need one**

**Definition**
- A fencing token is a number that increases every time a client acquires the lock. The lock service can do the incrementing. The client includes the token with every write request to the storage service. (Kleppmann, https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html)

**Failure scenario without a token** (the scenario you described, in the order it unfolds)
- Client A acquires a lock with a lease, for example 30 seconds. It then stalls, for example in a stop-the-world GC pause, a descheduled host, or a network partition. The lease expires and the lock service gives the lock to Client B. B writes to storage. A wakes up, still believes it holds the lock, and writes too. The result is stale or corrupt data. (https://dev.to/gabrielanhaia/design-a-distributed-lock-service-fencing-tokens-and-the-failure-modes-29nl)
- That article describes this as the core of Kleppmann's critique of using locks for correctness. It is a secondary source, not Kleppmann himself.
- Another secondary source says Kleppmann's post describes a real bug in a Redis-based locking library. A worker paused for a long GC, the lock expired, and a second worker took over. Both then wrote to the same row and corrupted the data. (https://hackernoon.com/building-distributed-leases-with-consensus-heartbeats-and-fencing-tokens)
- The point is that the lease alone cannot fix this. The holder cannot reliably know its lease has expired, because the pause can happen right after it checks. The lock service has already moved on without it.

**How the token fixes it**
- Kleppmann's example: Client 1 acquires the lease and gets token 33, then pauses for a long time and its lease expires. Client 2 acquires the lease and gets token 34. Client 2 writes to storage with token 34. Later Client 1 wakes up and sends its write with token 33. (Kleppmann, same URL as above)
- The storage server must take an active role. It checks the tokens and rejects any write whose token has gone backwards. Provided the lock service generates strictly monotonically increasing tokens, this makes the lock safe. (Kleppmann)
- In practice the resource remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects anything lower. That turns silent corruption into a detected and refused write. (https://sujeet.pro/articles/distributed-locking; secondary source)

**Caveats**
- Enforcement lives in the storage resource, not in the lock. A client-side check is not enough. Hazelcast states that all external services must take part in the fencing-token protocol, with guaranteed linearizability, for the setup to uphold its invariants. (https://hazelcast.com/blog/long-live-distributed-locks/)
- Hazelcast's FencedLock increments its token only when the lock moves from available to held. (same Hazelcast URL)
- Kleppmann's conclusion: if you need locks for correctness, use a proper consensus system such as ZooKeeper, and enforce fencing tokens on all resource accesses under the lock. He argues Redlock should not be used for this, because it has no fencing token. (Kleppmann)

**ZooKeeper, for the other specialists**
- Kleppmann says that with ZooKeeper as the lock service, you can use the zxid or the znode version number as the fencing token. (Kleppmann)

**Not found**
- The snippets I retrieved did not include Kleppmann's own prose on the GC-pause scenario, only the fencing section. I did not retrieve anything on etcd. I also did not retrieve his *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* chapter text. It is only cited as a source by https://github.com/mselser95/fencing-token-demo.

60eb0cbff0cc461a205f024c08659649bd752427.prompt_preview: Original question: How do Temporal, Celery and AWS Step Functions each detect a worker that dies in the middle of a task
60eb0cbff0cc461a205f024c08659649bd752427.text:
**Temporal: how it detects a dead worker and how it recovers** (from Temporal docs and the Temporal blog and forum)

**Activity failure detection**

- Temporal's docs list four mechanisms for detecting activity failures: Schedule-To-Start, Start-To-Close, Schedule-To-Close, and Activity Heartbeats. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- The server does not detect a worker crash or lost communication directly. Per the docs, it relies on the Start-To-Close Timeout to force Activity retries. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- Start-To-Close is the maximum time for a single Activity Task Execution. It has two uses: detecting that an individual worker crashed, and detecting that the worker fleet can't keep up. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- The docs say Temporal guarantees that an activity task either runs or times out. A task can be lost in delivery or after the function was called when the worker crashed. Temporal doesn't detect the loss directly and relies on Start-To-Close. https://docs.temporal.io/activity-execution
- Start-To-Close has no default. If only Schedule-To-Close is set, that value is used as Start-To-Close. If neither is set, the service rejects the activity. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- Heartbeats:
  - A heartbeat is a ping from the worker process to the Temporal Service. It tells the service the activity is making progress and the worker hasn't crashed. https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection
  - If no heartbeat arrives within the Heartbeat Timeout, the activity is considered failed. https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection
  - Heartbeats let a crash be detected faster than waiting for Start-To-Close. https://docs.temporal.io/design-patterns/long-running-activity
  - The docs recommend heartbeats and heartbeat timeouts for long-running activities. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- Schedule-To-Start is the time from scheduling to a worker picking up the task. It is mainly for detecting that the worker fleet is not keeping up, not a single crash. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
  - It is non-retryable by design. https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/activities/timeouts
  - Its default is infinity. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
  - Temporal recommends monitoring the `temporal_activity_schedule_to_start_latency` metric instead of setting it. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- Schedule-To-Close bounds the total time of an Activity Execution, including all retries. https://temporal.io/blog/activity-timeouts

**Activity recovery**

- When a timeout fires, the server records an ActivityTaskTimedOut event and attempts a retry according to the RetryPolicy. It puts the activity task back on the Activity Task Queue and increments the attempt count in the workflow's mutable state. https://temporal.io/blog/activity-timeouts
- Because the task goes back on the task queue, any available worker can pick it up. The docs say that after a crash and heartbeat timeout, Temporal retries the Activity on a new Worker. https://docs.temporal.io/design-patterns/long-running-activity
- The new attempt can read the last heartbeat details and resume from a checkpoint. https://docs.temporal.io/design-patterns/long-running-activity
- If no custom retry policy is given, a default one applies. It retries until a timeout threshold is reached. https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection
  - The activity doesn't return a failure to the workflow until that limit or a non-retryable condition is hit. https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection
  - The blog says that if allowed, Temporal retries for up to 10 years with backoff. https://temporal.io/blog/activity-timeouts
- If the retry policy allows only 1 attempt and a timeout occurs, the activity is not retried. https://docs.temporal.io/activity-execution
- When the heartbeat timeout fires, the last heartbeat details are returned to the workflow in the TimeoutError, with the timeout type set to Heartbeat. https://docs.temporal.io/develop/go/failure-detection

**Workflow task failures, sticky queues and replay**

- Workflow Tasks have their own `workflow_task_timeout`, a start-to-close timeout for how long a worker has to process the task. A WorkflowTaskTimedOut event exists. The event reference did not show the full field list in my results. https://docs.temporal.io/references/events
- Non-sticky queues: any worker polling the queue may take the next task. It receives the entire history and rebuilds workflow state by replaying from the start. https://github.com/temporalio/sdk-rust/blob/main/arch_docs/sticky_queues.md
- Sticky queues are a per-worker queue used to avoid shipping the full history and replaying every time. Unlike normal queues, they have a schedule-to-start timeout. https://github.com/temporalio/sdk-rust/blob/main/arch_docs/sticky_queues.md
- If the sticky worker is gone, that timeout lets the task fall back to the regular queue. A GitHub issue shows `StickyScheduleToStartTimeout` being set very low so that tasks from old sticky queues are rescheduled quickly after worker restarts. https://github.com/temporalio/temporal/issues/9118
- A Temporal forum answer, apparently from a Temporal staff member, says that after a workflow task fails or times out, the worker drops its cached state for that workflow (cache eviction). The server already holds the full history, so it needs no message from the worker. The workflow is no longer attached to the sticky queue. The next task is polled from the regular queue and the history is replayed. https://community.temporal.io/t/handling-workflow-task-timeout-due-to-sticky-queue-task-timeout/16443

**Gaps**
- I did not find an official page giving the default workflow task timeout (I recall 10 seconds, but I could not confirm it), the default sticky schedule-to-start timeout (I recall 5 seconds, also unconfirmed), or the default retry policy values.
- The retry-on-new-worker mechanism is described in docs and blog text. I did not find a separate page on the matching-service internals.

669780061c96b7fca00688e777a55cda6fa5d538.prompt_preview: Question: How does Concord decide that two subgoals are duplicates, and how does that differ from how semantic caches su
669780061c96b7fca00688e777a55cda6fa5d538.text:
**Short answer:** Concord's default check is an exact match on normalized text plus identical inputs. Embedding similarity is optional and off unless you supply an embedder. GPTCache's whole approach is embedding similarity, with an evaluator deciding whether a cached prompt matches.

**How Concord decides**
- Before dispatch, the supervisor checks each subgoal. It reuses an earlier duplicate's output if the subgoal has the "same normalized text and same inputs, or embedding similarity above a threshold" [README.md § What works today].
- Similarity matching is off by default: "Similarity matching is off unless an embedder is supplied" [README.md § Scorecard].
- The only embedder shipped is a word-overlap one meant for tests. It catches reordered or lightly edited subgoals, not true paraphrases [README.md § What works today].
- Measured results [README.md § Scorecard]:
  - Exact duplicates: 8/8 caught.
  - Reworded duplicates: 0/16 caught with the default settings.
  - With the word-overlap embedder switched on, light edits were caught 7/8 and 38/40 in a larger run. True paraphrases were caught 0/40.
  - In that larger run it reused the wrong output once in 40 look-alike runs, where two subgoals differed only in topic.
- Because of that wrong reuse, the word-overlap embedder stays off until a real embedding model is plugged in [README.md § Scorecard].
- A check has three possible outcomes, `dispatch`, `reuse` or `hold`. The span records which earlier subgoal it duplicates and why [tracing.md § Span reference].
- A duplicate served from an earlier result links to the span that produced it [tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgoal graph].

**How GPTCache decides** (source: https://zilliz.com/what-is-gptcache)
- It converts queries into embeddings and uses a vector store to find similar cached queries.
- The vector store returns the K most similar requests.
- A Similarity Evaluator module then compares the incoming request against those candidates, using data from the cache store and the vector store. Its result determines whether the request matches the cache.
- The evaluator uses pluggable strategies.
- The same page says semantic caching can give false positives and negatives.

**The differences**
1. **Default test.** Concord's default is a deterministic exact match on normalized text and inputs. GPTCache's default is semantic similarity, with a vector search followed by an evaluator.
2. **Inputs.** Concord requires the same inputs as well as the same text. I found no equivalent requirement in the GPTCache page I read. It matches on the prompt/query embedding.
3. **What is being cached.** Concord compares subgoals within a single run, and the reused output is a worker result on that run's blackboard. GPTCache compares incoming prompts against stored prompt-response pairs, and the cache store holds the LLM responses.
4. **Paraphrase handling.** Concord currently catches no paraphrases (0/16 with the default settings). Its planned fix is a real embedding model. GPTCache already supports real embedding models such as ONNX, SentenceTransformers and Cohere.

**What I couldn't find:** the page I read doesn't say what GPTCache's default similarity threshold is or what its default evaluator does. I also don't know how Concord normalizes text, because the passages don't say.
