a8e579a51013c81f351b19cab6c799bf1a0ae9a6.prompt_preview: Original question: How does Concord decide that two subgoals are duplicates, and how does that differ from how semantic
a8e579a51013c81f351b19cab6c799bf1a0ae9a6.text:
r was overwritten by the loop earlier.I could only get partial results. The search tool hit its usage limit after a few queries. I found nothing on GPTCache's specific evaluators (SearchDistanceEvaluation, ONNX), its default similarity thresholds, or how it returns a hit.

**GPTCache (architecture, from the ACL NLP-OSS paper)**
- GPTCache is an open-source semantic cache that stores and retrieves LLM responses. Unlike traditional caches such as Redis, it works through embeddings rather than exact keys. (https://aclanthology.org/2023.nlposs-1.24.pdf)
- It uses embedding algorithms to turn queries into vectors. It then runs similarity searches over those vectors in a vector store such as Milvus. (https://aclanthology.org/2023.nlposs-1.24.pdf)
- The paper describes six core components: adapter, pre-processor, embedding generator, vector storage, cache manager and similarity evaluator. The snippet I saw named only the adapter, pre-processor, embedding and vector storage ("stores embedding vectors and retrieves similar results"). The last two come from my memory of the paper, not from the snippet. (https://aclanthology.org/2023.nlposs-1.24.pdf)
- The snippet says users can customize the cache, with a range of choices for embeddings and other components. (https://aclanthology.org/2023.nlposs-1.24.pdf)

**Not established:** I could not verify the following GPTCache details.
- The evaluator class names and how each one computes similarity.
- The default threshold values.
- Whether the best match is returned when it passes the threshold.

**LangChain with Redis (RedisSemanticCache)**
- RedisSemanticCache stores and retrieves LLM responses by the semantic similarity of prompts rather than exact string match. It uses Redis vector similarity search. (https://reference.langchain.com/python/langchain-redis/cache/RedisSemanticCache)
- It takes an embedding function to encode prompts. The `distance_threshold` parameter defaults to 0.2 and is described as "the maximum distance for considering a cache hit". (https://reference.langchain.com/python/langchain-redis/cache/RedisSemanticCache)
- Lowering the threshold increases precision but may reduce cache hits. (https://reference.langchain.com/python/langchain-redis/cache/RedisSemanticCache)
- The older `langchain.cache.RedisSemanticCache` used `score_threshold=0.2`. Its docs say it was initialized "by passing in the init GPTCache func". Its `lookup(prompt, llm_string)` and `update(prompt, llm_string, return_val)` methods are keyed on both the prompt and the LLM configuration string. (https://sj-langchain.readthedocs.io/en/latest/cache/langchain.cache.RedisSemanticCache.html)
- LangCacheSemanticCache is a Redis managed-service variant. It has `distance_threshold` defaulting to 0.2, and `use_exact_search` and `use_semantic_search` both default to True. It also has a `distance_scale` option of 'normalized' or 'redis'. (https://reference.langchain.com/python/langchain-redis/cache/LangCacheSemanticCache)
- A tutorial describes the generic flow. It embeds the query and searches for stored embeddings within a distance threshold. A match returns the cached response, and a miss calls the LLM and then caches the query embedding and response. It calls the threshold the most important parameter to tune. (https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-17-how-to-implement-semantic-caching-with-langchain-and-memorystore-for-redis-on-gcp/view)
- A LangChain/Redis workshop issue notes that `score_threshold` was deprecated in favour of `distance_threshold`. A user there found that good values needed experimentation (0.9 with k=3 worked for them). (https://github.com/Redislabs-Solution-Architects/Redis-Workshops/issues/10)

**Summary for comparing with Concord**
- Semantic caches decide two prompts are "the same" by embedding similarity: embed the prompt, find the nearest stored vector, and accept it if the distance is under a configurable threshold.
- The threshold is a tunable cutoff, so the match is approximate and depends on the embedding model.

af0a815ae4bb3f00d022a7589541daa294df3d71.prompt_preview: Original question: What span names and attributes do the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define for agent invoc
af0a815ae4bb3f00d022a7589541daa294df3d71.text:
**Scope note:** I checked the official spec text only through search snippets, not the full pages. The inference attribute table is therefore only partly confirmed. I mark below what I could not verify.

**Where the spec lives**
- The GenAI conventions appear in two places. One is the main repo at v1.41.0: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/blob/v1.41.0/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md
- The other is a separate repo, `semantic-conventions-genai`, which has the same `docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md` file: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md
- A secondary source (hidekazu-konishi.com) says the GenAI conventions now live in the separate repo. I did not confirm this from an official page. https://hidekazu-konishi.com/entry/opentelemetry_genai_semantic_conventions_guide.html
- The attribute registry is at https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/registry/attributes/gen-ai.md

**Stability**
- The spans document is headed "Status: Development", and the Inference section is also marked Development. (semantic-conventions-genai gen-ai-spans.md, URL above)
- The well-known `gen_ai.operation.name` values and the `gen_ai.provider.name` values are each listed as Development. (same URL, and the registry URL)
- In the Embeddings table, `error.type` and `server.port` are listed as Stable. These are general attributes reused from elsewhere, not GenAI-specific. (same gen-ai-spans.md)
- A secondary source says all GenAI documents carry Development status. Another says that as of May 2026 the GenAI and MCP conventions remain in Development. https://hidekazu-konishi.com/entry/opentelemetry_genai_semantic_conventions_guide.html and https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions

**Inference span (model call)**
- The span represents a client call to a GenAI model or service that generates a response or requests a tool call. https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/blob/v1.41.0/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md
- The span name SHOULD be `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}`, for example `chat gpt-4`. Individual GenAI systems and frameworks MAY specify a different format. (same URL)
- Span kind SHOULD be CLIENT. It MAY be INTERNAL for models running in the same process. CLIENT is recommended when the GenAI system usually runs in a different process or the call goes over an instrumented protocol such as HTTP. (same URL)
- Span status SHOULD follow the Recording Errors document. (same URL)
- The OpenAI-specific page requires `gen_ai.provider.name` to be "openai" and says it SHOULD be set at span creation time. https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/openai.md

**`gen_ai.operation.name` well-known values**
These come from the spans document and the registry (URLs above). If one applies, it MUST be used. Otherwise a custom value MAY be used.
- `chat`: chat completion, such as the OpenAI Chat API.
- `text_completion`: text completions, such as the legacy OpenAI Completions API.
- `generate_content`: multimodal content generation, such as Gemini Generate Content.
- `embeddings`: embeddings, such as the OpenAI Create embeddings API.
- Other values are listed but are not model-call operations: `create_agent`, `execute_tool`, `create_memory`, `create_memory_store`, `delete_memory` and `delete_memory_store`. The spans document also has Retrievals (`retrieval`) and Fetch response sections.
- Where a specific system uses a different operation name, the spec RECOMMENDS documenting it in that system's conventions and using it in the instrumentation. Otherwise instrumentations SHOULD use the applicable predefined value.

**Inference attributes**
The full table is not in my snippets. I can confirm these:
- `gen_ai.operation.name` and `gen_ai.provider.name` are Required.
- `gen_ai.request.model` is Conditionally Required if available. A secondary source gives the same requirement levels for the inference span. https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router/issues/4140
- `error.type` is Conditionally Required if the operation ended in an error. The same level appears in the Embeddings table.
- `server.address` and `server.port` appear in the Inference attribute list. In the Embeddings table, `server.port` is Conditionally Required if `server.address` is set.
- That issue and the worked examples treat `gen_ai.response.model`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens` as Recommended. I did not see these rows in the official table itself.
- A secondary source also lists `gen_ai.conversation.id` and `gen_ai.output.type` as conditionally required. This is unverified against the official table. https://www.dash0.com/knowledge/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained
- Request-parameter attributes shown in secondary examples are `gen_ai.request.temperature`, `gen_ai.request.top_p`, `gen_ai.request.max_tokens` and `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons`. Example sources: https://openobserve.ai/blog/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions/ and https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions
- `gen_ai.response.id` appears in the same worked examples. The official Recommended or Opt-In levels for these were not verified.
- `gen_ai.system_instructions` is Opt-In. It appears in the agent-spans page snippet. https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md

**`gen_ai.provider.name` well-known values**
These include `anthropic`, `aws.bedrock`, `azure.ai.inference`, `azure.ai.openai`, `cohere`, `deepseek`, `gcp.gemini`, `gcp.gen_ai` and `gcp.vertex_ai`. The list is longer, and the snippet cut off. The spec says the attribute SHOULD be set from the instrumentation's best knowledge and may differ from the actual model provider. (registry and gen-ai-spans.md URLs above)

**Embeddings span**
- `gen_ai.operation.name` SHOULD be `embeddings`, and the name pattern is the same `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}`. https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/blob/v1.41.0/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md
- `gen_ai.provider.name` is Required, and `gen_ai.request.model` is Conditionally Required if available.
- `gen_ai.embeddings.dimension.count` (int) and `gen_ai.request.encoding_formats` (string[]) are Recommended. https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md

**Not established**
- I did not retrieve the official Recommended rows for the inference span: usage tokens, request parameters and finish reasons. The writer should open gen-ai-spans.md to confirm them.
- I did not confirm whether `gen_ai.provider.name` replaced `gen_ai.system`. A secondary source mentions a migration note. https://openobserve.ai/blog/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions/

b0c8f1c9e22be512c8ae11ace5b69aa43269c6aa.prompt_preview: Question: What delivery guarantees do Redis Pub/Sub, Redis Streams with consumer groups, and Apache Kafka consumer group
b0c8f1c9e22be512c8ae11ace5b69aa43269c6aa.text:
**Short answer:** Redis Streams with consumer groups is the lightest option that doesn't lose messages, provided Redis is already in your stack. Your project already uses it that way. Pub/Sub can lose messages across a restart. Kafka gives a similar guarantee but needs a whole extra system.

**Redis Pub/Sub: at-most-once, so a restart loses messages**
- Redis documents it as at-most-once. A message is delivered once if at all, and Redis never resends it. [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/pubsub/]
- If your subscriber wasn't attached at publish time, the message is gone. [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/pub-sub/dotnet/]
- A subscriber that is offline when a message is published misses it permanently. Redis suggests pairing Pub/Sub with durable state if you need replay. [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/pub-sub/nodejs/]

**Redis Streams with consumer groups: at-least-once, and the consumer resumes after a restart**
- Entries that have been delivered to a consumer but not yet acknowledged stay in a pending entries list. [https://redis.io/blog/simplifying-streams-and-strings/]
- The consumer calls `XACK` after processing, which lets Redis drop the entry from that list. [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/streaming/java-jedis/]
- After a restart, the consumer re-reads its pending entries by passing an explicit ID instead of `>`. `>` means "entries not yet delivered to anyone". [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/streaming/java-jedis/]
- A third-party guide (not Redis's own docs) describes this as at-least-once delivery even if a consumer crashes. [https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-redis-xreadgroup-consumer-groups/view]
- The catch is that an entry processed but not yet acknowledged when the consumer crashes will be delivered again. Handlers need to tolerate duplicates.

**Kafka consumer groups: at-least-once if you commit after processing**
- A consumer that takes over resumes from the last committed offset. It may repeat the last batch, which is what Kafka calls "at-least-once". [https://kafka.apache.org/10/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer/KafkaConsumer.html]
- Automatic offset commits can also give at-least-once. This only holds if you fully process everything each `poll` returns before the next `poll` or before closing. [https://kafka.apache.org/22/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer/KafkaConsumer.html]
- Committing offsets before processing would lose messages on a crash. Commit after processing. [https://www.conduktor.io/glossary/kafka-consumer-groups-explained]
- Exactly-once needs idempotent producers and transactional APIs (same Conduktor page). That is more than the other two options need.

**Which is lightest?** Redis Streams with consumer groups. It gives the same at-least-once guarantee as Kafka without a broker cluster. Your project already runs Redis, so it adds no new infrastructure.

**How this matches your project docs**
- ROADMAP.md says Redis Streams was chosen because Pub/Sub drops messages when the consumer is slow or restarting.
- README.md says the supervisor reads the event stream through a consumer group, so it resumes after a restart.
- The scorecard in README.md reports "Supervisor restart mid-run" at 8/8 correct. That is a measured result from the fault-injection harness. It covers the supervisor's restart, not a general proof of no loss.
- The last scorecard row says finished subgoals re-run after a crash is "not measured, recovery not built". So the at-least-once duplicate-delivery caveat above hasn't been checked in your system.

**What I didn't verify**
- I didn't find Redis's own page on pending-entry reclaim after a consumer dies permanently (`XAUTOCLAIM`/`XCLAIM`). If a consumer never comes back under the same name, you need that.
- The at-least-once label for Streams comes from a third-party page. Redis's docs describe the pending-list and `XACK` mechanism but, in what I retrieved, didn't use that label.

## What is confirmed

The blog title mentions timeouts, but that part was not read. | Not confirmed. |
| **CrewAI** | The Agents page summary describes `max_retry_limit` as retries on error. Its default was not seen. `max_iter` caps iterations before the agent must give its best answer (default 20). `max_rpm` limits requests per minute to avoid rate limits. ([CrewAI Agents docs](https://docs.crewai.com/v1.15.23/en/concepts/agents)) | `max_execution_time` is described as a timeout in seconds. Whether it stops a stuck step or only limits total time was not confirmed. ([same page](https://docs.crewai.com/v1.15.23/en/concepts/agents)) | Not confirmed. |
| **OpenAI Agents SDK** | Not confirmed. | Not confirmed. | Not confirmed. |

The OpenAI Agents SDK's `Runner.run` raises `MaxTurnsExceeded` when `max_turns` is exceeded "unless handled", and raises the matching tripwire exception, such as `InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered`, when a guardrail trips. This is a loop cap and a guardrail stop, not a retry or timeout. Only the opening snippet of the page was seen, so how the "unless handled" mechanism works is unconfirmed. ([Runner.run reference](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ref/run/))

## Gaps: not verified, so no claims are made

- **LangGraph:** the full `RetryPolicy` parameters and defaults, node timeouts, `recursion_limit`, checkpointers and resuming from the last checkpoint, and time travel and durable execution modes.
- **CrewAI:** task guardrails and their retry behavior, Flow error handling, Flow state persistence, crew replay from a task, and any other checkpointing.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK:** model and API retry settings, per-call or per-tool timeouts, tool-failure handling, session persistence, run-state serialization and resumption, durable-execution integrations, and whether any built-in checkpointing exists.

Because these were not found, I can't say whether any of the three frameworks lacks built-in support for a given feature. "Not confirmed" above means unchecked, not absent.

## Where to check next

- **LangGraph:** the persistence, durable execution, time travel and recursion-limit pages at docs.langchain.com, plus the [`RetryPolicy` API reference](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/types/RetryPolicy).
- **CrewAI:** the tasks, flows and CLI pages at docs.crewai.com.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK:** the running agents, sessions, guardrails, tools and human-in-the-loop pages at openai.github.io/openai-agents-python, plus the exceptions reference.

b439677be4d4200f37e3042b29344675a938f445.prompt_preview: Original question: What is the blackboard architecture in AI, where did it originate, and how have recent LLM multi-agen
b439677be4d4200f37e3042b29344675a938f445.text:
**Short answer:** The blackboard architecture is a problem-solving design in which independent specialist modules work together through a shared data store, with a control component deciding who acts next. It originated in 1970s AI research, in the Hearsay-II speech-understanding system at Carnegie Mellon. I could not verify how recent LLM multi-agent papers use it, because that part of the research failed. Details are below.

## What it is

The architecture has three components (https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0211029):
1. **Knowledge sources** are independent, modular subsystems. Each holds specific knowledge about part of the problem domain and represents a different point of view or strategy.
2. **The blackboard** is a shared data structure. It holds the facts and deductions produced during problem solving, and it is the only channel through which the knowledge sources communicate (https://wiki.tcl-lang.org/page/Blackboard+Systems).
3. **A control mechanism** decides the order in which knowledge sources operate on the blackboard.

Knowledge sources respond opportunistically to changes on the blackboard, and their contributions build up step by step into a solution. Because of this, control has to decide at each moment which action to take (https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0211029).

Nii and Brown's Stanford slides add detail. The blackboard is organized into levels, nodes and links, with a vocabulary for each level. Control is event-based, scheduling knowledge sources according to the current situation (https://stacks.stanford.edu/file/druid:nh044zx3884/nh044zx3884.pdf).

One description gives a four-step workflow (https://klu.ai/glossary/blackboard-system):
- initialization
- activation of relevant knowledge sources
- execution
- conflict resolution

The style suits problems with no fixed solution path, such as speech understanding, and it lets diverse techniques be integrated without dependencies between knowledge sources (https://www.academia.edu/1848568/Blackboard_Systems). The "uncertain or noisy data" framing is the specialist's own inference from the Hearsay-II paper title.

## Where it came from

- AI researchers conceived it in the 1970s to handle shared information among multiple expert agents. It was first developed in the Hearsay-II language-understanding system (https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0211029).
- The standard citation is Erman, Hayes-Roth, Lesser & Reddy (1980), "The HEARSAY-II speech understanding system: Integrating knowledge to resolve uncertainty". Lesser & Erman (1977) is also cited (https://stacks.stanford.edu/file/druid:xq803jt6713/xq803jt6713.pdf).
- In Hearsay-II the input was a digitized spoken sentence, to be interpreted as a legal sequence of words. Knowledge sources contributed hypotheses at levels such as acoustic features, words and syntax (https://stacks.stanford.edu/file/druid:nh044zx3884/nh044zx3884.pdf, https://klu.ai/glossary/blackboard-system).
- Later systems adapted the CMU model. These include HASP, Protean and CRYSALIS, plus the AGE environment (https://stacks.stanford.edu/file/druid:nh044zx3884/nh044zx3884.pdf, https://stacks.stanford.edu/file/druid:xq803jt6713/xq803jt6713.pdf).
- Penny Nii's "The blackboard model of problem solving" (AI Magazine 7(2), 1986) is the standard survey (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/13437.13438).
- Barbara Hayes-Roth's BB1, developed at Stanford, added control of the system's own behavior (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00140399). Her 1985 paper "A blackboard architecture for control" is about this later system, not Hearsay-II itself.
- Rick Hayes-Roth is described as a co-inventor of Hearsay-II and the blackboard architecture (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Hayes-Roth).

**Not established:** the exact dates of the Hearsay-II project, the roles of individual team members, details of HASP/SIAP, and which system first used the term "blackboard". These rest on memory only, so I have left them out.

## Recent LLM multi-agent papers

I have no verified findings here. The search tool failed for this part. The only lead is a paper titled "Exploring Advanced LLM Multi-Agent Systems Based on Blackboard Architecture", which has a third-party summary page (https://www.themoonlight.io/en/review/exploring-advanced-llm-multi-agent-systems-based-on-blackboard-architecture). Its likely arXiv ID is 2507.01701, but that ID was only seen as a search result, not read. I did not read the summary or the paper, so I cannot report its authors, design or results, and I have not identified any other papers.

The mapping to the classic design is therefore untested. It is plausible that LLM agents stand in for knowledge sources and a shared message or memory space stands in for the blackboard. Whether these papers keep the classic opportunistic, event-driven control is not confirmed. Check the paper itself before relying on that comparison.

b64741b9bd2f17115b2d04ff5d8eb2802d5cffc6.prompt_preview: Original question: How does Jaeger's clock skew adjustment work, when does it change span timestamps, and how can it be
b64741b9bd2f17115b2d04ff5d8eb2802d5cffc6.text:
**Short answer:** Jaeger's query service adjusts span timestamps when it returns a trace. It only shifts a child span that falls outside its parent's time bounds and comes from a different host. The shift is capped by a maximum. You turn it off by setting that maximum to `0s`: `--query.max-clock-skew-adjustment=0s` in v1, or `max_clock_skew_adjust: 0s` on the `jaeger_query` extension in v2. Since v1.20 it is off by default. Parts of the algorithm could not be confirmed (see the end).

**How it works**
- **Where it runs.** The adjustment runs in the query service, not in the browser or at storage time. The query service applies its standard adjusters "before returning the data to the API clients" (https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/cmd/query/app/querysvc). Clock skew is one of those adjusters. In v2 the list comes from `StandardAdjusters(maxClockSkewAdjust)` (https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/cmd/query/app/querysvc/v2/adjuster). I infer that stored data is not rewritten, but no source says so outright.
- **Why it exists.** Traces combine data from hosts whose clocks drift. Skew can make a server span appear to start before its client span, which should be impossible. The algorithm uses the causal relationships between spans (https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/).
- **What it checks.** The code comments say it modifies start times and log timestamps of spans that look "off" relative to their parent. The main condition is that child spans must not start before or end after their parents (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.46.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go).
- **How it walks the trace.** It builds a tree of spans from parent references and adjusts from each root, carrying a skew value down the tree. It assumes span IDs are unique, so the span-ID deduplication adjuster runs first (same file).
- **How the shift is chosen.** If a child already fits inside its parent, nothing changes and the delta is 0 (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.59.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go). Otherwise the child is repositioned in the middle of its parent. Jaeger can't know the real request/response latency split, so it assumes they are equal (https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/).
- **Cross-host only.** Spans from the same host are not expected to need adjustment.
  - In v2, a host key is derived from resource attributes such as `host.id`, `host.ip` or `host.name` (https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/cmd/query/app/querysvc/v2/adjuster).
  - For v1, a user in issue #1459 says the host was identified by the process `ip` tag, with a missing tag treated as a different host (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/1459). That is a user description, not documentation.

**When it does not change timestamps**
- The calculated delta exceeds the configured maximum. The span is left alone and a warning is recorded: "max clock skew adjustment delta of %v exceeded; not applying calculated delta of %v" (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.67.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go).
- Adjustment is disabled. The warning is "clock skew adjustment disabled; not applying calculated delta of %v" (same file).
- Span IDs are duplicated or parent span IDs are invalid. Adjustment is skipped (same file). Issue #2121 reports the invalid-parent warning, and the reporter guessed the cause was a child reaching the collector before its parent (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/2121).
- The adjuster never returns errors. It records problems in `Span.Warnings` (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.46.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go).

**How you can tell**
Every adjusted span shows a UI warning with the exact skew delta applied (https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/).

**Turning it off**
- **v1.** Set `--query.max-clock-skew-adjustment=0s`. The help text says 0s disables adjustment (https://github.com/orgs/jaegertracing/discussions/2712).
- **v2.** Set `max_clock_skew_adjust: 0s` on the `jaeger_query` extension (https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/2.22/deployment/configuration/).
- **Default.** Since v1.20 the default is 0s, so adjustment is off unless you enabled it. That change was breaking (https://newreleases.io/project/github/jaegertracing/jaeger/release/v1.20.0) and came from PR #2513, which fixes #1459, "Clock Skew Adjuster considered harmful" (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/pull/2513). To enable it, set a non-zero duration such as `5s`.
- **Scope.** The setting is server-wide, applying to all traces from that query service (https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/). A UI toggle is still an open ticket (#197) (https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/2.22/deployment/configuration/). I found no per-adjuster switch. Issue #1367 asked for one, but I couldn't confirm it was implemented (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/1367).
- **Unverified.** A third-party blog mentions the environment variable `QUERY_MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_ADJUSTMENT`, which I could not check against Jaeger docs (https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-06-resolve-clock-skew-opentelemetry-distributed-traces/view).

**Discrepancies and gaps**
- **Docs vs. default.** The 1.20 deployment docs describe the algorithm as running and the flag as controlling it, but don't make the 0s default explicit. The default comes from the release notes and discussion #2712.
- **v2 behavior.** Issue #6565, "Max clock skew setting not applied in v2", reports the YAML key being accepted but apparently not taking effect. I did not see how it was resolved, and the v2 default value was not found (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/6565).
- **Algorithm internals not read.** I could not read the body of `adjustNode`. These points are therefore unconfirmed:
  - The exact shift formula. It is likely (parent duration − child duration)/2, but that is a guess.
  - Whether descendants inherit the shift.
  - How a missing host key is handled in v2.
- **Known criticism.** Issues #961 and #1459 call the adjuster surprising and only a best guess, and ask for a way to see raw data (https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/961).

bca0fda1c39725cf34321cb17c6c062f6724321b.prompt_preview: Original question: How do Temporal, Celery and AWS Step Functions each detect a worker that dies in the middle of a task
bca0fda1c39725cf34321cb17c6c062f6724321b.text:
I have enough for a report. Some parts are only partly sourced.

**Celery: detecting a worker that dies mid-task, and recovering**

**Detection: a prefork child process dies**
- With the prefork pool, the main worker process monitors its child processes. If a child is killed, for example by OOM SIGKILL, the parent logs that the ForkPoolWorker process exited with "signal 9 (SIGKILL)". It then marks the task as failed with `WorkerLostError('Worker exited prematurely: signal 9 (SIGKILL).')`. Sources: https://github.com/celery/billiard/issues/380 and https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/5690. The traceback in the billiard issue shows this raised from `mark_as_worker_lost` in `billiard/pool.py`.
- The parent then spawns a replacement child. The container and the main worker keep running, so Kubernetes reports nothing. Source: https://engineering.backmarket.com/a-story-of-kubernetes-celery-resource-and-a-rabbit-ec2ef9e37e9f
- The configuration docs describe `worker_lost_wait`. A worker killed without cleanup may already have published a result. This setting says how long to wait for a missing result before raising `WorkerLostError`. Source: https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html

**Default recovery behaviour (acks_late=False)**
- By default, a message is acknowledged just before the task runs. Source: https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/reference/celery.app.task.html
- So if the worker dies mid-task, the broker has already discarded the message. The task is not re-run automatically. It is reported as failed with `WorkerLostError` in the result backend. This follows from the doc statement above and the logs in the issues cited. I did not find one sentence in the docs that says this outright.

**acks_late and reject_on_worker_lost**
- With `acks_late=True`, the message is acknowledged after the task has run. The docs warn that the task may be executed twice if the worker crashes mid-execution. Source: https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/reference/celery.app.task.html
- You can set it globally with `task_acks_late`. Same source.
- Even with `acks_late` on, the worker acknowledges the task when the child process executing it abruptly exits or is signaled (KILL, INT and so on). Source: https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/reference/celery.app.task.html
- The task docs say that if you want the task redelivered in these cases, you should enable `task_reject_on_worker_lost`. Source: https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html
- Wolt's engineering blog recommends combining `acks_late=True` with `reject_on_worker_lost=True`. It also notes that `visibility_timeout` matters in the `acks_late` case. Source: https://careers.wolt.com/en/blog/tech/5-tips-for-writing-production-ready-celery-tasks
- A user reported that with this setting on, a SIGTERM-killed task is rescheduled. But `AsyncResult.get()` still raises `WorkerLostError`. Source: https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/4229 (a user issue, not official docs).
- A recent PR describes an edge case. If a child dies after the task has already succeeded, the parent gets `WorkerLostError`. The errbacks then fire, and with `reject_on_worker_lost` the task is requeued even though it already ran. Source: https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/10752

**Node-level death (whole worker or machine lost) and the visibility timeout**
- Unacknowledged messages are redelivered when the broker connection closes. They are also redelivered when the visibility timeout is exceeded. Source: https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v5.5.1/history/whatsnew-3.0.html
- For Redis, if a task isn't acknowledged within the visibility timeout, it is redelivered to another worker and executed. The default is 1 hour. It is set via `broker_transport_options = {'visibility_timeout': ...}`. Source: https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/getting-started/backends-and-brokers/redis.html
- The Redis docs also say Celery redelivers messages at worker shutdown. So a long visibility timeout only delays redelivery of "lost" tasks after a power failure or a forcefully terminated worker. Same source.
- The Wolt post says the visibility timeout applies to the Redis and SQS transports.
- Side effect: a task that runs longer than the visibility timeout can be picked up by a second worker while the first is still running it. Source: https://dev.to/artemooon/celery-redis-at-scale-designing-a-reliable-and-efficient-task-queue-in-production-27nh

**Not established**
- My last two searches hit a tool limit. I did not retrieve the Celery docs on `broker_heartbeat`, or on RabbitMQ detecting a dead consumer. That is the mechanism where the broker notices a TCP drop or missed heartbeat and requeues unacked messages. The whenever-the-connection-closes redelivery claim above comes only from the 3.0 "what's new" page, not from a RabbitMQ or heartbeat source.
- I did not confirm the exact current default of `task_reject_on_worker_lost`. The docs page shows `None`, which I read as off unless set.
- Celery has no central supervisor that tracks tasks in flight. Detection depends on the parent process and on the broker's ack and connection semantics. This is my inference from the sources, not a sourced statement.
- I did not cover retries (`autoretry_for`, `task.retry`). They only apply to exceptions raised inside the task, not to a lost worker, which is likewise my inference.

c590c085626ccfc3073c1e55d027358bf8e6082f.prompt_preview: Original question: According to Concord's own scorecard, which failures does its supervisor catch and which does it miss
c590c085626ccfc3073c1e55d027358bf8e6082f.text:
**Short answer:** Concord's supervisor, by its own scorecard, reliably catches exact duplicate subgoals and dead workers, and it has no detection for off-task output. It also misses reworded duplicates by default. The most-cited published taxonomy (MAST) puts step repetition, reasoning-action mismatch, termination unawareness and spec violations at the top. Concord overlaps with that list only on repetition, and only in its exact form.

## What the scorecard says

The scorecard comes from 72 scripted fault-injection runs, each with one injected fault, played with and without the supervisor. Everything ran on a mock model, so token figures are word counts and only relative differences mean anything. [README.md § Scorecard]

**Caught**
- **Exact duplicate subgoals:** 8/8 (100%). The duplicate never reaches a worker, and 11.2% of tokens were saved on runs with one. This works because a pre-dispatch check (pending → checking → ready → leased → done) compares normalized text and inputs before any worker spends tokens. [README.md § Scorecard; ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- **Dead worker:** 8/8 correct with the supervisor, versus 0/8 without (the run hangs). Detection took about 0.4s at worst, against a ≤0.80s target. The supervisor requeues subgoals whose worker stopped sending heartbeats. [README.md § Scorecard, § What works today]
- **Supervisor restart mid-run:** 8/8. It reads events through a Redis consumer group, so it resumes after a restart. [README.md § Scorecard, § What works today]
- **False alarms on healthy runs:** 0/16, against a target of ≤5%. [README.md § Scorecard]
- **Light edits to duplicates:** caught only if the optional word-overlap embedder is on (7/8 here, 38/40 in a larger run). [README.md § Scorecard]
- **Hung worker:** 8/8 correct, but with or without the supervisor. The worker's own deadline catches it, not the supervisor. [README.md § Scorecard]

**Missed**
- **Reworded duplicates:** 0/16 by default, against a ≥90% target. Similarity matching is off unless an embedder is supplied. [README.md § Scorecard]
- **True paraphrases:** 0/40, even with the word-overlap embedder. That embedder is for tests, and a real embedding model is planned for a later phase. [README.md § Scorecard, § What works today]
- **Wrong reuse:** with the word-overlap embedder on, the supervisor reused the wrong output once in 40 look-alike runs, where subgoals differed only in topic. [README.md § Scorecard]
- **Off-task output:** 0/8, with or without the supervisor. There is no drift check yet. The target was precision and recall ≥0.8, and the check is planned as Phase 6. [README.md § Scorecard; ROADMAP.md § Roadmap]
- **Not measured:** finished subgoals re-run after a crash, because recovery is not built (Phase 7). [README.md § Scorecard]

The README says the reworded-duplicate and off-task gaps are left in on purpose. [README.md § Scorecard]

The inputs do not give the similarity threshold, the lease durations beyond the "2 × lease" target, or how the token budget is counted. The intended scope is 5 to 20 subgoals, parallel readers, one writer. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]

## What published studies say

The only quantified taxonomy found is MAST, from "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" (Cemri et al.). It has 14 failure modes in three categories, built on 1,642 annotated traces, with failure rates of 41% to 86.7% across 7 open-source systems. (https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2503.13657; https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657)

Versions of the paper disagree. An early version (about 200 traces) gave category shares of 41.8% specification, 36.9% inter-agent misalignment and 21.3% verification. (https://futureagi.substack.com/p/why-do-multi-agent-llm-systems-fail) The later version gives 44.2%, 32.3% and 23.5%. (https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2503.13657; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.17915) I use the later figures.

Most frequent individual modes, later version:
- Step repetition: 15.7%.
- Reasoning-action mismatch: 13.2%.
- Unaware of termination conditions: 12.4%.
- Disobey task specification: 11.8%.
- Incorrect verification: 9.1%.
- No or incomplete verification: 8.2%.
- Task derailment: 7.4%.

(https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.17915; https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2503.13657; https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3)

A PDF snippet shows different per-mode numbers, such as step repetition at 37.17%. I could not confirm what subset those come from, so treat them as unverified. (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13657)

IBM's ITBench post reports reasoning-action mismatch in 92% of failures for one model. The snippet did not say which model, so check it before citing. (https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-research/itbenchandmast)

## Comparison

**Overlaps**
- **Step repetition** (the top MAST mode) is the nearest match to Concord's duplicate-subgoal detection. Concord covers only exact duplicates reliably, and 0% of reworded ones by default.
- **Task derailment** (7.4%) resembles Concord's off-task output, which it misses entirely.
- **Stalled or dead agents:** Concord's dead-worker detection is a strong result, but nothing in the MAST frequency list maps to it directly.

**Gaps**
- Concord has no check for reasoning-action mismatch, termination unawareness, spec or role violations, or verification failures. Verification failures together are roughly a quarter of MAST failures. Its token budget halt is the only termination-related control described, and that is a cost guard, not a check on whether agents know when to stop.
- Concord's scorecard does not test several of MAST's major categories.

**Caveats**
- The categories are not like-for-like. MAST labels behaviours seen in traces from 7 open-source systems. Concord's scorecard measures 72 scripted, single-fault injections on a mock model. Injected faults are not naturally occurring failures, so Concord's detection rates say nothing about how often each fault happens in the wild.
- Concord's infrastructure failures (dead worker, supervisor restart) are largely outside MAST's agent-behaviour categories.
- Concord's intended scope (5 to 20 subgoals, parallel readers, one writer) is narrower than the MAST systems.
- I found no independent second taxonomy with its own frequency table, so "published studies" here effectively means MAST and work that reuses it.

ccd4688b3411b259c1324245ec361353ddb95e33.text:
I could only run one search before the tool limit was hit, and that search returned just a short excerpt. My findings are therefore partial.

**Established, from the official Langfuse data model page** (https://langfuse.com/docs/observability/data-model):
- Langfuse organizes data into three core concepts: observations, traces and sessions.
- Observations are the individual steps of an application, such as LLM calls, tool calls and retrieval steps. They can be nested to reflect the application's structure.
- Langfuse supports several LLM-specific observation types, including generations and events. It calls spans observations, and span is also a specific observation type.
- A trace represents a single request or operation, for example one chatbot interaction from the user's question to the final response.
- Trace-level attributes such as user_id, session_id, tags and metadata live on every observation within the trace. The SDKs propagate them automatically.
- The page's example table shows observation-level data (id, type, name, latency) alongside trace-level data (trace_id, trace_name, user_id) repeated on every row.

**Not established.** I did not retrieve or verify any of the following:
- The definition of a session, beyond the session_id attribute above.
- The newer observation types for agents, such as agent, tool, chain and retriever.
- How Langfuse represents multi-agent workflows, including any agent graph view.
- How OpenTelemetry ingestion maps to traces and observations, including the attribute mapping and the OTLP endpoint.

The writer should not state any of these points from my report. They would need a further look at the Langfuse docs on observation types, the OpenTelemetry integration and agent graphs.

cf15a4889b38e22df24039d5dce37088e349b255.prompt_preview: Original question: What mechanisms do the Claude API, the OpenAI API and LangGraph provide for capping the tokens or ste
cf15a4889b38e22df24039d5dce37088e349b255.text:
**Claude API: mechanisms for capping tokens or steps**

1. **`max_tokens` (per request).**
   - It is a required parameter on Messages API calls. The compatibility docs describe it as the maximum number of tokens to generate before stopping, and an absolute maximum. The model may stop earlier. (https://mimo.mi.com/docs/en-US/api/chat/anthropic-api — this is a third-party compatibility page that reproduces the Anthropic parameter description, not Anthropic's own docs.)
   - When the cap is hit, `stop_reason` is `max_tokens`. (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons; the snippet shown only checks for this value, and the page's stop-reason list is truncated.)
   - It caps output for one request only. It is not a cumulative budget across an agent loop. The sources I found don't say so explicitly, so that is my inference from how the parameter works.

2. **Extended thinking `thinking={"type":"enabled","budget_tokens":N}`.**
   - It sets a target for how many tokens Claude can use for internal reasoning. (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking)
   - The minimum is 1,024 tokens, and the API rejects smaller values. (same page)
   - `budget_tokens` must be less than `max_tokens`, because thinking tokens count toward the `max_tokens` limit for the turn. (same page)
   - The exception is interleaved thinking. There, `budget_tokens` can exceed `max_tokens` because the budget spans all thinking blocks within one assistant turn. (same page)
   - The docs call the budget a target, not a strict cap. Actual usage varies, and Claude may stop reasoning well before the budget. (same page)
   - A third-party note from pydantic-ai says Anthropic rejects a request whose `max_tokens` isn't greater than the budget. (https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/pull/8986)
   - LangChain's docs say Opus 4.6+ can use adaptive thinking, which determines the budget automatically. Sonnet and earlier models need an explicit token budget. (https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/chat/anthropic)

3. **`max_uses` on the server-side web search tool.**
   - It is an optional parameter on the tool definition, for example `{"type":"web_search_20250305","name":"web_search","max_uses":5}`. It limits the number of searches per request. (https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/web-search-tool)
   - The current docs describe it as a hard constraint on searches per request. Prompting alone only steers how readily Claude searches. (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/web-search-tool)
   - If Claude tries more searches than allowed, the `web_search_tool_result` is an error with the `max_uses_exceeded` error code. (same page)
   - I did not verify whether other server tools, such as web fetch or code execution, have an equivalent parameter. I did not search for that.

4. **Tool runner iteration limit in the SDK.**
   - The SDK's tool runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner(...)`) loops until Claude returns a message with no tool use. It also stops at `max_iterations` if you set it. (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-runner)
   - You can also `break` out of the loop at any iteration. (same page)
   - By the wording of that page, the iteration limit is optional and has no default cap. I only saw the Python examples and did not confirm the parameter's exact name or availability in the TypeScript, Go or other SDKs.
   - The tool runner appears to be in the beta namespace, as in the Python example `client.beta.messages.tool_runner`. The docs snippet didn't state this beyond that.

**Not found**
- I found no API-level mechanism that caps cumulative tokens or turns across a manually written tool-use loop. In a manual loop, the developer's own code has to count iterations and usage. This is an absence of evidence in my searches, not a documented statement.
- I did not find the full text of the `pause_turn` stop reason. It is relevant to server-tool loops, but I can't report on it.

d071332e302c81cea4486b87f657e4281027f20c.prompt_preview: Original question: What positions do Anthropic's 'How we built our multi-agent research system' and Cognition's 'Don't B
d071332e302c81cea4486b87f657e4281027f20c.text:
Not the primary. Try again.I could only read part of Anthropic's post directly. Search returned the opening and a few passages from anthropic.com. The remaining detail comes from secondary sources that quote or summarize the post. I could not retrieve the full primary text, so I have marked what is directly from Anthropic and what is secondhand.

**Directly from Anthropic's post (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)**
- The post defines a multi-agent system as multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together. In the Research feature, an agent plans a research process from the user's query. It then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information at the same time. Anthropic says multi-agent systems introduce new challenges in agent coordination, evaluation and reliability.
- Subagents work in parallel, each with its own context window. They explore different aspects of the question at once, then condense the most important tokens for the lead research agent.
- Each subagent also separates concerns: distinct tools, prompts and exploration trajectories. Anthropic says this reduces path dependency and enables independent investigations.
- Its general argument is that once model intelligence passes a threshold, multi-agent systems become a vital way to scale performance. It compares this to human societies becoming more capable through collective intelligence and coordination.
- The post says multi-agent research systems excel especially at breadth-first queries that pursue multiple independent directions at once.

**Quoted from the post by Slashdot (https://developers.slashdot.org/story/25/06/21/0442227/anthropic-deploys-multiple-claude-agents-for-research-tool---says-coding-is-less-parallelizable)**
- The post says multi-agent architectures scale token usage for tasks that exceed the limits of a single agent.
- The cost: agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more.
- Anthropic says multi-agent systems excel at valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization, information that exceeds single context windows, and interfacing with numerous complex tools.
- Anthropic names coding as a weaker fit. Most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelizable pieces than research, and LLM agents are "not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time."
- The post says multi-agent systems work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem.

**Secondary sources quoting or summarizing the post**
- Fountain City quotes Anthropic's limit: "domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today." (https://fountaincity.tech/resources/blog/anthropic-multi-agent-blueprint-production/)
- Performance (Simon Willison quoting the post, https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/14/multi-agent-research-system/): a system with Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research eval.
- Several secondary summaries say the same thing. The comparison is on Anthropic's internal eval, and the lead was Opus 4 with Sonnet 4 subagents.
  - Morph says the lead was Opus 4 with Sonnet 4 subagents. (https://www.morphllm.com/ai-agent-orchestration)
  - 13labs also notes the multiple-token-budget caveat: the multi-agent system was allowed to spend roughly 15 times as much. (https://www.13labs.au/guides/multi-agent-orchestration-what-works)
- Token usage explaining performance (Medium and Beri summaries, https://www.beri.net/learning/anthropic-multi-agent-research-system): on the BrowseComp evaluation, token usage alone explained about 80% of performance variance. Three factors (token usage, number of tool calls, model choice) explained about 95%.
- Model choice (Medium summary, https://medium.com/@packapun/lessons-from-anthropics-multi-agent-research-system-e312314e997f): upgrading to Sonnet 4 gave a bigger gain than doubling the token budget on Sonnet 3.7.
- Architecture (several secondary summaries, e.g. https://www.13labs.au/guides/multi-agent-orchestration-what-works): the lead agent running Opus 4 plans the approach and saves the plan to memory. It then spawns parallel Sonnet 4 subagents, each with its own context window and tool access. A separate citation agent then ties the results to sources (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/how-anthropic-built-a-multi-agent).
- Context persistence (ZenML summary, https://www.zenml.io/llmops-database/building-a-multi-agent-research-system-for-complex-information-tasks): the memory system persists context when conversations exceed 200,000 tokens.
- Prompting lessons (summaries of the post, https://medium.com/@kushalbanda/how-we-built-our-multi-agent-research-system-5f5e10b2a8d6 and https://www.13labs.au/guides/multi-agent-orchestration-what-works):
  - Early versions spawned 50 subagents for simple queries and searched endlessly for nonexistent sources. Agents also distracted each other with excess updates.
  - Vague delegation, such as "research the semiconductor shortage," led to duplicated work. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, tool guidance and clear task boundaries.
  - Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort, so Anthropic embedded scaling rules in the prompts. Simple fact-finding gets 1 agent with 3–10 tool calls. Direct comparisons get 2–4 subagents with 10–15 calls each. Complex research gets more than 10 subagents. (AgentPatterns.ai gives the same 1 / 2–4 / 10+ tiers: https://agentpatterns.ai/patterns/multi-agent/orchestrator-worker/)
  - Anthropic found prompting was the main lever, using simulations to watch agent behavior step by step. (https://theaiengineer.substack.com/p/how-anthropic-built-multi-agent-deep)
- Artifacts instead of a "game of telephone" (Medium summary): subagents write outputs to a filesystem rather than routing everything through the lead agent. I only saw a truncated snippet of this one. (https://medium.com/@packapun/lessons-from-anthropics-multi-agent-research-system-e312314e997f)
- Tool-description testing (same Medium summary): Anthropic reportedly cut task completion time by 40% through tool ergonomics testing.
- Parallel tool calls (summary by evoailabs, https://evoailabs.medium.com/multi-agent-research-anthropic-119e8952886a): parallel tool calls cut research time by up to 90%. This is a secondary claim I could not check against the primary text.

**Not established**
- My search budget ran out before I could confirm from primary text the post's statements on:
  - stateful error compounding
  - rainbow deployments
  - synchronous-execution bottlenecks
  - the "3–5 subagents" figure (one secondary source, theaiengineer, mentions it)
  - the exact wording of its prompting principles
- I also did not confirm the post's date from the primary source. 13labs says 13 June 2025, and Simon Willison's post is dated 14 June 2025.

d0950c3ec44cc94c50b9c61bbee51cecccef153c.prompt_preview: Question: What does Concord's supervisor do before a subgoal is dispatched, and how does that differ from the supervisor
d0950c3ec44cc94c50b9c61bbee51cecccef153c.text:
Before a subgoal is dispatched, Concord's supervisor checks it for duplicates. If an earlier subgoal has the same normalized text and the same inputs, or an embedding similarity above a threshold, the supervisor reuses that earlier output. The subgoal never reaches a worker. [README.md § What works today]

**How it works in Concord**
- In a supervised run, a subgoal moves `pending → checking → ready → leased → done`. A duplicate is therefore caught before any worker spends tokens on it. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- Inputs are part of the comparison. The same instruction applied to different inputs counts as different work. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- Each check shows up as a `concord.supervisor.check` span. Its `concord.blackboard.dispatch` child is the write that puts the subgoal in the worker queue. [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]
- A duplicate served from an earlier result links to the span that produced that result. [tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgoal graph]
- Measured on the mock model, exact duplicates were caught 8/8 times. Runs with an exact duplicate used 11.2% fewer tokens. [README.md § Scorecard]
- Reworded duplicates are not caught by default, at 0/16. Similarity matching is off unless an embedder is supplied. [README.md § Scorecard]
- The shipped word-overlap embedder catches light edits but not true paraphrases. In one larger run it also reused the wrong output once in 40 look-alike runs. [README.md § Scorecard]

The supervisor also requeues subgoals whose worker stopped sending heartbeats, halts a run that goes over its token budget, and logs every intervention. [README.md § What works today]

**Difference from LangGraph's supervisor pattern**
I can't answer this half from the material you gave me. None of the passages describes LangGraph, and I did not search, so I won't characterize its supervisor from memory. To compare the two, check the LangGraph documentation on its supervisor or multi-agent pattern. One thing to check is whether its supervisor routes work to agents instead of screening each subgoal before dispatch.

The Concord passages do say that specialists are a plain model-and-tool loop. A graph framework would be added only where a specialist needs branching. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions] That is about specialists, not a comparison with LangGraph's supervisor.

d29af0cdd7965bd701dc4e64b5acbc2ac0ba8c3d.prompt_preview: Original question: How do Temporal, Restate and DBOS each implement durable execution, and what does each require of the
d29af0cdd7965bd701dc4e64b5acbc2ac0ba8c3d.text:
**How DBOS implements durable execution**

- DBOS is a library you install into your own application. You annotate workflows and steps, and while the app runs, DBOS checkpoints them to a Postgres database. After a crash, interruption or restart, it recovers each workflow from its last completed step. https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture
- Every workflow input and step output is durably stored in the system database. https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture
- DBOS uses Postgres to orchestrate durable workflows and queues. There is no separate orchestration server, and no infrastructure is needed beyond Postgres. https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture
- Application servers talk directly to Postgres, with no central orchestrator in between. A client submits a workflow by creating a row in a workflows table. Servers poll the table and dequeue workflows to run, using locking clauses so that each workflow is dequeued by exactly one worker. https://www.dbos.dev/blog/postgres-is-all-you-need-for-durable-execution
- Each worker checkpoints step outputs to Postgres itself. If several workers try to run the same workflow, Postgres integrity constraints let them detect the duplicate on checkpoint and back off. https://www.dbos.dev/blog/postgres-is-all-you-need-for-durable-execution
- If a server crashes, another server can recover its workflows from their checkpoints. https://www.dbos.dev/blog/postgres-is-all-you-need-for-durable-execution

**Recovery, in three steps** (https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture)
1. DBOS detects interrupted workflows.
   - In a single-node deployment this happens automatically at startup, when DBOS scans for incomplete (PENDING) workflows.
   - In a distributed deployment some coordination is needed, either automatic through a service like DBOS Conductor or done manually.
2. DBOS restarts each interrupted workflow by calling it again with its checkpointed inputs. Before each step, the workflow checks whether that step's output is checkpointed. If it is, the step returns the stored output instead of running.
3. The recovered workflow eventually reaches a step with no checkpoint. This is where the original execution failed, and execution continues normally from there.

**What DBOS requires of developer code**
- **Decorators or annotations.** In Python you mark functions with `@DBOS.workflow()` and `@DBOS.step()`. https://docs.dbos.dev/why-dbos
  - Other languages have equivalents (Java, Go and others have their own docs). In Go and Java the app is configured with a Postgres system database URL or datasource. https://docs.dbos.dev/golang/tutorials/workflow-tutorial
- **Deterministic workflows.** Given the same arguments and step return values, a workflow must invoke the same steps with the same inputs in the same order. Non-deterministic operations must go in steps. Examples are database access, third-party API calls, random numbers and reading the local time. https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture
  - Workflows can otherwise use ordinary loops, branches and conditionals. https://docs.dbos.dev/python/tutorials/workflow-tutorial
  - DBOS raises `DBOSStepNondeterminismError` if one execution of a workflow recorded different results for the same step. https://docs.dbos.dev/python/tutorials/workflow-tutorial
- **Idempotent steps.** Steps should be safe to retry. If a workflow fails mid-step, that step is retried during recovery. Once a step has completed and been checkpointed, it is never re-run. https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture
  - A step can therefore execute twice if the failure happens during it, so DBOS says steps should be idempotent or resilient to re-execution. https://www.dbos.dev/blog/why-postgres-durable-execution
  - Steps are guaranteed at-least-once by default. DBOS claims exactly-once for steps that only do database operations. It does this by running the step inside one Postgres transaction that also writes the checkpoint. https://www.dbos.dev/blog/why-postgres-durable-execution
  - Setting a workflow ID makes it an idempotency key. Calling a workflow several times with the same ID executes it only once. Workflow IDs must be globally unique within the application. https://docs.dbos.dev/python/tutorials/workflow-tutorial
- **Postgres dependency.** Postgres is the system database, and the Java step factories check that the datasource is PostgreSQL. https://docs.dbos.dev/java/reference/workflows-steps
  - The Pydantic AI integration docs say DBOS also supports SQLite, but recommend Postgres for production. https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/capabilities/durable_execution/dbos/
  - Throughput is bounded by how fast the database can process workflows, and availability depends on the database being available. https://www.dbos.dev/blog/postgres-is-all-you-need-for-durable-execution
- **Versioning and code changes.**
  - A breaking change is one that changes which steps run or their order. Checkpoints from the old code may then not match the new code, and recovery can fail. https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture
  - DBOS offers two strategies: patching and versioning. With patching you add patch statements so a breaking change sits inside a conditional and old workflows can still recover. https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture
  - With versioning, each workflow is tagged with the application version it started on. By default the version is a hash of the workflow source code, and you can set your own. https://docs.dbos.dev/golang/tutorials/workflow-tutorial
  - Recovery only picks up workflows whose version matches the current application version. DBOS recommends blue-green deploys: keep old-version processes running until their workflows drain. https://docs.dbos.dev/java/tutorials/upgrading-workflows
- **Distributed deployments.** Recovery needs coordination, through DBOS Conductor or manual handling (see step 1 of recovery above). https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture

**Not established in my searches**
- I did not find a precise statement of DBOS's per-step write overhead or limits on checkpoint size.
- I did not verify that every language SDK (Python, Java, Go, TypeScript) matches on every detail. Most of the detail above comes from the Python, Go and Java docs.

d7a9081db9bdda7004f7659ea661215d6ea332cb.prompt_preview: Original question: How does Jaeger's clock skew adjustment work, when does it change span timestamps, and how can it be
d7a9081db9bdda7004f7659ea661215d6ea332cb.text:
Let me get the rest of the code and the v2 docs.I only got partway: the search tool hit its use limit before I could read the core of the algorithm in `clockskew.go`. What's established and what isn't:

**Established**

- Jaeger's docs say the backend combines trace data from applications that usually run on different hosts, whose hardware clocks often drift relative to each other (clock skew). Source: https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/
- The same page says clock skew can make a server span appear to start earlier than its client span, which should not be possible. The query service runs the adjustment algorithm, and it uses knowledge of causal relationships between spans. Source: https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/ (The v2 docs make the same statement for the `jaeger_query` extension: https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/2.dev/deployment/configuration/)
- The docs say all adjusted spans show a warning in the UI giving the exact clock skew delta applied to their timestamps. Source: https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/
- The docs give a limitation. When Jaeger moves a server span inside its parent's bounds, it doesn't know the split between request and response latency, so it assumes they are equal and centres the child in the parent. Source: https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/ (this is tied to issue #961)
- The docs name the flag that controls this. `--query.max-clock-skew-adjustment` controls how much adjustment is allowed, and setting it to 0s disables adjustment completely. Source: https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/ (Other specialists may cover the v2 option name. I did not confirm it.)
- Code comments in `clockskew.go` (v1.46.0) say the adjuster modifies start time and log timestamps for spans that look "off" relative to the parent span because of clock skew on different servers. Source: https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.46.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- The same file says the main condition it checks is that child spans do not start before or end after their parent spans. Source: https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.46.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- The file says the algorithm assumes span IDs are unique, so another adjuster such as SpanIDDeduper may need to run first. It also says the adjuster never returns errors and records problems in `Span.Warnings`. Source: https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.46.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- The structure, from the same file:
  - It builds a map of span nodes and then subgraphs.
  - For each root it calls `adjustNode(n, nil, skew)`, starting from a skew keyed on the node's `hostKey`.
  - `hostKey` is the host-identity field. I did not see how it is computed, so I can't confirm it comes from IP/hostname attributes.
- Warning strings in the source (v1.67.0) show when the adjustment is skipped or not applied:
  - duplicate span IDs
  - invalid parent span IDs
  - max delta exceeded ("not applying calculated delta")
  - adjustment disabled ("not applying calculated delta")
  
  Source: https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.67.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- GitHub issue #2121 reports the "invalid parent span IDs…; skipping clock skew adjustment" warning. The reporter guessed the cause was a child span reaching the collector before its parent. Source: https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/2121
- Issues #961 ("Make clock skew adjustment transparent") and #1459 ("Clock Skew Adjuster considered harmful", a duplicate of #961) criticise the adjuster. Their complaint is that it is surprising and only gives a best guess. They ask for a toggle to show raw data. Sources: https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/961 and https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/1459
- #1459 says the algorithm compares durations, which only makes sense if the spans are roughly the same size. I only saw a snippet of it.
- PR #9767 changed `adjustNode` from recursive to an explicit-stack walk. The reason was that very deep traces could overflow the goroutine stack. The visit order and skew propagation stayed the same, and each sibling starts from its parent's skew. Source: https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/pull/9767
- The v2 code lives in `cmd/query/app/querysvc/v2/adjuster`. It has `CorrectClockSkew(maxDelta time.Duration)`, `StandardAdjusters(maxClockSkewAdjust)`, `DeduplicateClientServerSpanIDs()` and `NormalizeIPAttributes()`. Source: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/cmd/query/app/querysvc/v2/adjuster

**Not established (searches ran out)**

- I did not read the body of `adjustNode` or the `clockSkew` struct. So I can't confirm from the source:
  - how the skew delta is computed (for example, that the child is centred using `(parentDuration - childDuration)/2`)
  - whether skew is propagated to descendants and log timestamps
  - how `hostKey` is derived
  - the exact conditions that trigger a change, beyond "child starts before or ends after its parent on a different host"
- I did not confirm the exact v2 config key for the max skew setting, or its default. The v1.20 docs only show the `--query.max-clock-skew-adjustment` flag.

e0e1cf6b23e03e38a46f7f9dc21be9f058201a19.prompt_preview: Original question: What does Concord's supervisor do before a subgoal is dispatched, and how does that differ from the s
e0e1cf6b23e03e38a46f7f9dc21be9f058201a19.text:
I did not find LangGraph's own supervisor tutorial page in these results. They draw on the langgraph-supervisor reference/README (primary) and third-party tutorials (secondary).

**What the supervisor does before dispatch**

- The langgraph-supervisor library has a `create_supervisor` function that builds a supervisor agent to orchestrate several specialized agents. Its features include a "tool-based agent handoff mechanism". https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py
- Handoffs are tools. `create_handoff_tool` makes a tool that hands control to a named agent. The supervisor LLM picks a handoff tool by calling it. https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph-supervisor
- By default the handoff tool passes the full message history to the subagent. You can customize it to add tool-call arguments for the LLM to fill in, such as a task description for the next agent. You can also change what data the subagent receives. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py
- `create_supervisor` takes a `model`, a `prompt`, optional extra `tools`, `add_handoff_messages`, `handoff_tool_prefix` and `response_format`. https://www.langgraphcn.org/reference/supervisor/
- Handoff tool descriptions help the supervisor decide when to use each tool. The default description is generic, and a LangGraph JS issue asked for per-agent custom descriptions. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraphjs/issues/1509
- Hand-built supervisor (tutorial style): the supervisor node is a function that prepends a system prompt to the message state and calls `llm.with_structured_output(Router)`. `Router` is a TypedDict whose `next` field is a `Literal` of worker names plus FINISH. The node then returns `Command(goto=...)`, mapping FINISH to END. https://blog.futuresmart.ai/multi-agent-system-with-langgraph
- Another tutorial's router also includes a `reasoning` field, so the LLM explains its routing choice. The node writes `next` and the query into state. https://medium.com/@anuragmishra_27746/building-multi-agents-supervisor-system-from-scratch-with-langgraph-langsmith-b602e8c2c95d
- Another tutorial uses a `SupervisorDecision` Pydantic model with `next_agent: Literal[...]`. It says the Literal constraint stops the LLM from inventing a node name such as "sleep_agent". https://shafiqulai.github.io/blogs/blog_15.html
- The supervisor can also be a plain routing function. One tutorial has the supervisor write `next_agent` into state. A conditional-edge function then returns that value, or "finalize" if `task_complete` is set. https://medium.com/@n.raki2331/building-a-supervisor-architecture-with-langgraph-orchestrating-multiple-ai-agents-add5ba193763
- Another tutorial describes a supervisor step that reads whether research, analysis and a report already exist in state and names the next agent. This is the closest thing in these sources to a state check. It is a routing heuristic, not a validation step. https://www.krishnaik.in/ai-tutorials/langgraph/multi-agent
- Workers are typically compiled subgraphs or agents used as nodes in the supervisor's graph. https://guatemalia.com/en/blog/multi-agente-langgraph-patrones-supervisor-trabajadores.html

**Validation or planning before dispatch**

- None of the sources describes a built-in validation or planning gate in LangGraph's supervisor pattern. The supervisor makes one LLM decision (a tool call or structured output) and the graph transitions to that worker.
- The only guard found is schema-level. The `Literal` type restricts the output to known worker names (shafiqulai link above). That checks the name of the worker, not whether the subgoal is sound or feasible.
- The optional `reasoning` field is a justification the LLM writes, not a check.
- Any pre-dispatch checks, such as plan validation, would have to be added by the developer as extra nodes or conditional edges. I did not find a documented example of this.

**Caveats**

- These sources are mostly tutorials and blogs, not the official LangGraph docs. The reference and README for langgraph-supervisor are the primary sources.
- "No validation" is an absence of evidence in the sources I searched, not a statement from LangGraph's docs.

e46205d5a0d364dbf3f5c7890a25424c6605c4d4.prompt_preview: Original question: What does Concord's supervisor do before a subgoal is dispatched, and how does that differ from the s
e46205d5a0d364dbf3f5c7890a25424c6605c4d4.text:
Findings on what the Concord supervisor does before a subgoal is dispatched (from the project documents only):

**Pre-dispatch steps**

- The supervisor checks each subgoal before dispatch. [README.md § What works today]
- In a supervised run, a subgoal moves through the states `pending → checking → ready → leased → done`. The checking state sits before ready and leased, so a duplicate is caught before any worker spends tokens on it. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- The check reuses the output of an earlier duplicate. A duplicate is defined as the same normalized text and the same inputs, or embedding similarity above a threshold. [README.md § What works today]
- Duplicate detection combines a normalized key with embedding similarity, because repeated subgoals usually arrive reworded. Inputs are part of the comparison: the same instruction applied to different inputs counts as different work. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
- The shipped embedder is a word-overlap embedder for tests. It catches reordered or lightly edited subgoals, not true paraphrases; those need a real embedding model, planned for the real-model phase. [README.md § What works today]
- Task drift is checked with a yes/no rubric tuned on a labelled set, not a raw score. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions] The passages do not say whether this drift check runs in the pre-dispatch stage or elsewhere, nor whether it is implemented yet.

**Tracing of the pre-dispatch step**

- Each pre-dispatch check is recorded as a `concord.supervisor.check` span. Each has a `concord.blackboard.dispatch` child, which is the write that put the subgoal in the worker queue. [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]
- A duplicate served from an earlier result links to the span that produced that result. [tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgoal graph]
- Supervisor interventions are logged as `supervisor.*` events with a reason. [README.md § What works today]

**Related checks that happen before the supervisor stage (not supervisor actions)**

- Graph validation on submission: the graph must be acyclic, reference only known subgoals, and stay within size and depth limits. [README.md § What works today]
- The planner checks its own plan (no cycles, exactly one writer, no work that reaches no answer) and sends a rejected plan back once with the reason. [README.md § What works today]
- Scheduling releases a subgoal when all its dependencies are done. The passages attribute this to scheduling, not to the supervisor. [README.md § What works today]

**Other supervisor duties (not pre-dispatch)**

- It requeues subgoals whose worker stopped sending heartbeats, and halts the run when it exceeds its token budget. [README.md § What works today]
- It reads the event stream through a consumer group, so it resumes after a restart. [README.md § What works today]

**Not established by the passages**

- Specialist assignment: the passages do not say the supervisor assigns a subgoal to a specialist before dispatch.
- Whether the token-budget check happens at the pre-dispatch point or continuously.
- Anything about the LangGraph supervisor pattern; the passages do not mention LangGraph. The only related note is that specialists are a plain model-and-tool loop, with a graph framework added only where a specialist needs branching. [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]
