ebe3384ddd6f2024978084c453fcaa76a470afe3.prompt_preview: Original question: How do Temporal, Restate and DBOS each implement durable execution, and what does each require of the
ebe3384ddd6f2024978084c453fcaa76a470afe3.text:
**Short answer:** Restate and DBOS are covered below with sources. Temporal could not be sourced, so its section is a gap rather than an answer.

- **Restate** is a server that sits in front of your services and journals every step.
- **DBOS** is a library that checkpoints workflows and steps to Postgres, with no separate server.
- Both recover by re-running code and returning recorded results for steps that already finished. Both require that non-deterministic work be wrapped in a durable step.

## Temporal

The research on Temporal failed. Every search hit a tool limit, so there are no sourced findings. I am not filling this from memory. The mechanism, determinism rules, activity/workflow split, worker model and versioning are all unestablished here. Pages that were listed as consulted but not read or verified include https://docs.temporal.io/workflows, https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/event-history and https://docs.temporal.io/develop/dotnet/workflows/versioning. Anyone relying on this answer should check the official Temporal docs directly.

## Restate

**Mechanism**
- Restate is a server plus a thin SDK in your service. It acts like a message broker or reverse proxy in front of your handlers (https://docs.restate.dev/tour/workflows). Handlers can be invoked over HTTP, Kafka or typed clients (https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/handlers).
- Every external interaction is recorded to a persistent log before the application sees the result. After a crash the engine restarts the function and replays the journal, and completed steps return their recorded results (https://restate.dev/what-is-durable-execution).
- The server keeps a bidirectional connection to the running handler. Its view of the invocation and journal is the ground truth (https://restate.dev/blog/building-a-modern-durable-execution-engine-from-first-principles).
- Internally (https://docs.restate.dev/references/architecture):
  - Ingress routes a call to a partition leader by workflow ID, virtual-object key or idempotency key.
  - The durable log, "Bifrost", commits a write when a quorum of replicas acknowledges it.
  - A per-partition processor tails the log and invokes handlers. It keeps a materialized cache in embedded RocksDB holding journals, state and timers.
  - State is snapshotted to S3 for bounded recovery. Snapshots also let the log be trimmed (https://docs.restate.dev/server/snapshots).

**Service types** (https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/services)
- Basic Service: stateless handlers.
- Virtual Object: keyed state with a single writer per key.
- Workflow: a `run` handler that executes once per ID, plus concurrent shared handlers and workflow promises.

**Developer code requirements**
- Handlers use a Restate `ctx`, whose type depends on the service type (https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/handlers).
- External calls and non-deterministic operations such as database writes and API calls are wrapped in `ctx.run(...)` (https://restate.dev/what-is-durable-execution, https://docs.restate.dev/tour/workflows). The same applies to LLM and tool calls in agents (https://docs.restate.dev/ai/patterns/durable-agents).
- State goes through `ctx.get` and `ctx.set`, and calls to other services go through the context (https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/services, https://docs.restate.dev/tour/workflows).
- Saga compensations are written by the developer using `ctx.run` (https://docs.restate.dev/tour/workflows).
- Inputs and outputs must be JSON-serializable (https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/handlers).
- Code is deployed as an HTTP endpoint and registered with the server (https://docs.restate.dev/services/versioning).

**Versioning**
- Deployments are immutable. Each version gets its own endpoint, in-flight invocations stay on their original version, and new requests go to the latest (https://docs.restate.dev/services/versioning).
- Re-registering the same URI is an error (META0004). Forcing it can leave in-flight invocations unrecoverable, so it is acceptable only in local development (https://docs.restate.dev/references/errors).
- Handlers that run for days or months force you to keep old deployments around. The docs recommend splitting the work into smaller chunks with delayed calls (https://docs.restate.dev/services/versioning).

**Gaps:** I found no source stating the determinism rules, such as deterministic time, random and UUID helpers, or what happens when replay diverges from the journal. The pages imply handler code must be deterministic outside `ctx.run`, but none says so. I also found nothing on awakeables or durable promises beyond workflow promises, and nothing on `ctx.run` retry semantics.

## DBOS

**Mechanism**
- DBOS is a library installed in your application. You annotate workflows and steps, and it checkpoints them to Postgres. After a crash it recovers each workflow from its last completed step (https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture).
- Every workflow input and step output is stored in the system database. No orchestration server is needed beyond Postgres (https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture).
- A client submits a workflow by inserting a row in a workflows table. Servers poll the table and dequeue with locking clauses so that exactly one worker takes each workflow. Workers checkpoint their own steps, and Postgres integrity constraints let duplicate executors detect each other and back off (https://www.dbos.dev/blog/postgres-is-all-you-need-for-durable-execution).
- Recovery (https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture):
  1. Interrupted (PENDING) workflows are detected. This is automatic at startup on a single node. A distributed deployment needs coordination, either DBOS Conductor or manual.
  2. Each is re-invoked with its checkpointed inputs. Steps with stored outputs return them instead of running.
  3. Execution continues normally from the first step with no checkpoint.

**Developer code requirements**
- **Annotations:** in Python, `@DBOS.workflow()` and `@DBOS.step()` (https://docs.dbos.dev/why-dbos). Go and Java have equivalents and are configured with a Postgres URL or datasource (https://docs.dbos.dev/golang/tutorials/workflow-tutorial).
- **Deterministic workflows:** the same arguments and step results must lead to the same steps, with the same inputs, in the same order. Database access, API calls, random numbers and reading the time belong in steps (https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture). Ordinary loops and branches are allowed (https://docs.dbos.dev/python/tutorials/workflow-tutorial). `DBOSStepNondeterminismError` is raised when one execution of a workflow recorded different results for the same step (same page).
- **Idempotent steps:** a step interrupted mid-run is retried on recovery, but a checkpointed step is never re-run (https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture). Steps are at-least-once by default. DBOS claims exactly-once only for database-only steps, which run in one Postgres transaction together with the checkpoint (https://www.dbos.dev/blog/why-postgres-durable-execution). Setting a workflow ID makes it an idempotency key (https://docs.dbos.dev/python/tutorials/workflow-tutorial).
- **Postgres dependency:** Postgres is the system database (https://docs.dbos.dev/java/reference/workflows-steps). SQLite is also supported but not recommended for production (https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/capabilities/durable_execution/dbos/). Throughput and availability are bounded by the database (https://www.dbos.dev/blog/postgres-is-all-you-need-for-durable-execution).
- **Versioning:** a breaking change is one that alters which steps run or their order. There are two strategies (https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture):
  - Patching puts the change inside a conditional so old workflows can still recover.
  - Version tagging labels each workflow with its application version, by default a hash of the source (https://docs.dbos.dev/golang/tutorials/workflow-tutorial). Recovery only picks up workflows matching the current version, so DBOS recommends blue-green deploys that let old processes drain (https://docs.dbos.dev/java/tutorials/upgrading-workflows).

**Gaps:** I found no per-step write overhead or checkpoint-size limits. Detail comes mostly from the Python, Go and Java docs, and parity across all language SDKs is unverified.

## Comparison

| | Temporal | Restate | DBOS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Architecture | Not sourced | Separate server in front of your services, with a SDK in your code | Library in your app, no orchestrator |
| Storage | Not sourced | Replicated log (Bifrost) with RocksDB state and S3 snapshots | Postgres, plus SQLite for non-production use |
| Recovery | Not sourced | Journal replay | Re-invoke the workflow and skip checkpointed steps |
| Code constraints | Not sourced | Side effects go in `ctx.run`; state and calls go through `ctx`; determinism is implied but unsourced | Deterministic workflows, idempotent steps, side effects go in steps |
| Versioning | Not sourced | Immutable deployments per version | Patching or version-tagged blue-green |

- **Shared pattern:** both systems re-run your code on recovery and substitute recorded results for completed steps. That is why both push non-deterministic work into a wrapped step.
- **Main difference:** Restate adds an infrastructure component and handles versioning by routing to old deployments. DBOS adds only a database dependency and handles versioning through code patches or version-matched recovery.
- **Missing:** a comparison against Temporal cannot be made until its sourced research is done.

ec68411fce81fcbdc1d20a1fa6bd2c2b4a5e922d.prompt_preview: Original question: How do Temporal, Celery and AWS Step Functions each detect a worker that dies in the middle of a task
ec68411fce81fcbdc1d20a1fa6bd2c2b4a5e922d.text:
Findings on AWS Step Functions (my part only). Search limits stopped me from fetching the official error-handling page directly, so the Retry/Catch details come from secondary sources and are marked below.

**How Step Functions detects a dead or unresponsive worker**

- Step Functions has no health check on the worker itself. It detects failure through timeouts and missed heartbeats.
  - When a task starts, it waits for a success or failure response from the task or activity worker within `TimeoutSeconds`. If none arrives, the task fails. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html
  - For Activities, the timeout clock starts when `GetActivityTask` hands out a token and `ActivityStarted` is logged. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html
- `HeartbeatSeconds` is the second detection mechanism, and it catches a dead worker sooner than the overall timeout does.
  - The doc describes it as the frequency of heartbeat signals an activity worker sends. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html
  - It must be a positive integer smaller than `TimeoutSeconds`. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html
  - If more time than that passes between heartbeats, the Task state fails with a `States.Timeout` error. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html
  - Heartbeats are sent with `SendTaskHeartbeat`. Activity workers and callback-pattern tasks can use it to report that the task identified by the token is still making progress. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSJavaSDK/latest/javadoc/com/amazonaws/services/stepfunctions/AWSStepFunctionsClient.html
- The default for both `TimeoutSeconds` and `HeartbeatSeconds` is 99,999,999. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html
  - Without an explicit timeout, Step Functions often relies solely on a response from an activity worker. A task with no `TimeoutSeconds` can therefore sit stuck waiting for a response that never comes. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/sfn-best-practices.html
  - A secondary source says a hung activity will wait "a year (max timeout) at least" without a timeout. https://serverlessguru.medium.com/aws-step-functions-a-users-guide-f8d313dfdfeb
- Activity workers poll with `GetActivityTask`, a long poll that the service holds open for up to 60 seconds. It returns a `taskToken` identifying the scheduled task. That token must be used in later `SendTaskHeartbeat`, `SendTaskSuccess` or `SendTaskFailure` calls. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/apireference/API_GetActivityTask.html
  - Workers can pass an optional `workerName`, which is logged in the execution history. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/apireference/API_GetActivityTask.html
- For callback patterns (`.waitForTaskToken`), the best-practices page recommends adding `HeartbeatSeconds`. If it is set below the task timeout, a heartbeat failure tells you the task failed rather than ran long. The example passes the token as `$$.Task.Token`. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/sfn-best-practices.html
- Activity workers report results with `SendTaskSuccess` or `SendTaskFailure`, using the task token. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-activities.html

**Error names**

- `States.Timeout` is raised when a task runs longer than `TimeoutSeconds` or fails to send a heartbeat within `HeartbeatSeconds`. https://dashbird.io/blog/aws-step-functions-error-handling/
- `States.TaskFailed` is raised when a Task state fails for any reason. The same source says it also covers function timeouts and out-of-memory errors for Lambda. https://dashbird.io/blog/aws-step-functions-error-handling/
  - These are secondary sources (Dashbird, Serverless Guru). The official `state-task` page confirms the `States.Timeout` behaviour for both timeouts and heartbeats.
- A `States.ALL` matcher in Catch or Retry cannot catch `States.Runtime` errors. https://dashbird.io/blog/aws-step-functions-error-handling/

**How it recovers: Retry and Catch**

- `Retry` is a list of retrier objects, each with `ErrorEquals`, `IntervalSeconds`, `MaxAttempts` and `BackoffRate`.
  - Secondary source: `IntervalSeconds` is the wait before the first retry, 1 second by default. https://dev.to/dashbird/aws-step-functions-error-handling-49d0
  - Secondary source: `MaxAttempts` defaults to 3, and `0` means never retry. https://dashbird.io/blog/aws-step-functions-error-handling/
  - Secondary source: `BackoffRate` is the multiplier applied to the interval on each attempt, 2.0 by default. https://dashbird.io/blog/aws-step-functions-error-handling/
  - Example: with `IntervalSeconds: 2` and `BackoffRate: 2.0`, the first retry waits 2 seconds and the second waits 4. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-12-handle-errors-retries-step-functions/view
- Once retries are exhausted, normal error handling resumes. https://dashbird.io/blog/aws-step-functions-error-handling/
  - A secondary example shows a retrier hitting its `MaxAttempts` for an error and the execution then being redirected through `Catch` to another state. https://dev.to/dashbird/aws-step-functions-error-handling-49d0
- `Catch` routes to a fallback state with `ErrorEquals` and `Next`, and optionally `ResultPath` to attach the error info to the input. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-12-handle-errors-retries-step-functions/view
  - You can use separate `Catch` entries, for example `States.Timeout` to a timeout handler and `States.TaskFailed` to a different one. https://dev.to/aws-builders/mastering-aws-step-functions-error-handling-j39
  - A Timeout catch commonly leads to a `Fail` state or a compensation or notification step. https://dev.to/aws-builders/mastering-aws-step-functions-error-handling-j39
- Retriers are evaluated in order, so put specific ones before `States.ALL`. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-12-handle-errors-retries-step-functions/view
- Timeouts can be retried. One example uses a `States.Timeout` retrier with `IntervalSeconds: 10`, `MaxAttempts: 2` and `BackoffRate: 1.0`. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-12-handle-errors-retries-step-functions/view
  - On a retry, the task is scheduled again. For an Activity, that makes a new task available to the next `GetActivityTask` poll, so another worker can pick it up. This is my inference; I did not find it stated explicitly in what I read.

**Not established**

- I did not retrieve the official "Handling errors" / Retry-Catch page. The defaults above (1 second, 3 attempts, 2.0) come from Dashbird, not AWS docs.
- I did not verify `MaxDelaySeconds`, `JitterStrategy`, or the claim that retries count as state transitions for billing.

ecab2dd5e00c9db7b96dfe295c9b6ba8d6dd8182.prompt_preview: Original question: What span names and attributes do the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define for agent invoc
ecab2dd5e00c9db7b96dfe295c9b6ba8d6dd8182.text:
Results are dicts in a string? Let me search for official pages.Get the primary doc.**Agent spans in the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions**

**Where the spec lives now**
- The GenAI conventions have moved out of the main semantic-conventions repo. The opentelemetry.io semconv index (v1.44.0) says "Generative AI: Moved to the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions repository." https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/
- The current agent-span document is `docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md` in open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai. https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md
- A secondary source says the old opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/ pages are now redirect stubs. https://www.dash0.com/knowledge/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained
- The v1.41.0 snapshot of the old repo is at https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/blob/v1.41.0/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md

**Agent span types defined**
The agent-spans document lists these sections: Create agent span, Invoke agent client span, Invoke agent internal span, Invoke workflow span, Plan span, Execute tool span, and agent-skill spans (Load skill, Read skill resource, Command execution). https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md

**Create agent span**
- Status is Development, and the requirement level is Recommended. It describes agent creation and usually applies to remote agent services.
- `gen_ai.operation.name` SHOULD be `create_agent`.
- The span name SHOULD be `create_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}`. Individual GenAI system or framework conventions MAY specify a different format.
- Span kind SHOULD be CLIENT.
- Attributes, all Development stability except `error.type`:
  - `gen_ai.operation.name`: Required.
  - `gen_ai.provider.name`: Required.
  - `error.type`: Conditionally required if the operation ended in an error. Its stability is Stable.
  - `gen_ai.agent.description`: Conditionally required if provided by the application.
  - `gen_ai.agent.id`: Conditionally required if applicable. It is the stable unique identifier of the agent. For hosted agents it SHOULD be the provider-assigned stable identifier, such as an AWS Bedrock agent ARN or a GCP Agent Registry identifier. Recording in-memory agent instance ids on it is NOT RECOMMENDED.
  - `gen_ai.agent.name`: Conditionally required if provided by the application.
  - `gen_ai.agent.version`: Conditionally required if provided by the application.
- Source: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md. The attribute table and the `gen_ai.agent.id` note come from the opentelemetry.io registry search snippet, which I did not open in full.

**Invoke agent client span**
- It describes agent invocation over a remote service.
- `gen_ai.operation.name` SHOULD be `invoke_agent`.
- The span name SHOULD be `invoke_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}` if the agent name is readily available. Otherwise it SHOULD be `invoke_agent`. Frameworks MAY specify a different format.
- Span kind SHOULD be CLIENT.
- Source: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md

**Invoke agent internal span, Invoke workflow span, Plan span**
- These sections exist (`invoke_workflow` and `plan` are operation values). I did not retrieve their span names or attribute tables.
- The older text said invoke-agent span kind SHOULD be CLIENT and MAY be INTERNAL for in-process agents. The GitHub issue quoting that text is https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/issues/308. The newer split into separate client and internal sections appears to replace it.

**`gen_ai.operation.name` values**
- The registry lists these values, all with Development stability: `chat`, `create_agent`, `embeddings`, `execute_tool`, `generate_content`, `invoke_agent`, `invoke_workflow`, `retrieval`, `text_completion`.
- The main-branch `gen-ai-spans.md` adds `plan`, the memory operations (`create_memory`, `create_memory_store`, `delete_memory`, `delete_memory_store`, `search_memory`, `update_memory`, `upsert_memory`) and others.
- Sources: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/registry/attributes/gen-ai/ and https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md

**Related spans, for the other specialists**
- Execute tool span kind SHOULD be INTERNAL (v1.41.0 doc, https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/blob/v1.41.0/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md).
- The inference span name is `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}`, for example `chat gpt-4` (secondary source, https://www.dash0.com/knowledge/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained).
- One secondary source (Greptime) says that from v1.41 the tool name must appear in the tool span name, as `execute_tool {gen_ai.tool.name}`. I did not verify this in the primary spec. https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions

**Stability**
- The Create agent span is marked "Status: Development". Every `gen_ai.*` attribute and operation value above is Development. The only Stable item is the generic `error.type`.
- A secondary source says the spec is still marked Development (https://www.dash0.com/knowledge/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained).
- One blog (jacar.es) claims the names are "consistent" after a 2025 "stabilisation window". That does not contradict the official Development marking, and I would not treat it as evidence of stable status. https://jacar.es/en/agent-observability-with-opentelemetry-genai-semconv-in-2026/

**Not established**
- I did not retrieve the full attribute table for invoke agent (client or internal), invoke workflow or plan spans. Likely attributes include `gen_ai.agent.id`, `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`, but only a secondary source says so (https://www.morphllm.com/agent-tracing). Check the primary file for the exact requirement levels.

ecc91cc99e3b35918e97c43d165d1a4cb57482ea.prompt_preview: Question: How does Concord model a multi-agent run as an OpenTelemetry trace, and how do Langfuse and Arize Phoenix mode
ecc91cc99e3b35918e97c43d165d1a4cb57482ea.text:
**Short answer:** Concord puts a whole multi-agent run in one OpenTelemetry trace with a flat structure. Attempts are siblings, and span links express the dependencies. Langfuse and Phoenix both model a run as a nested tree of typed spans. The sources I found don't describe how either one handles dependencies between sibling agents, so I can't compare that.

**Concord** [tracing.md, docs/tracing.md in the project]
- One run is one OpenTelemetry trace. The trace context travels through the blackboard as W3C `traceparent` strings, so spans from different workers and from the supervisor join the same trace.
- The root span is `invoke_workflow {name}`. Each attempt is an `invoke_agent {agent}` span. Model calls are `chat {model}` spans and tool calls are `execute_tool {tool}` spans. Supervisor checks, requeues and blackboard writes are `concord.*` spans.
- Every attempt is a direct child of the root span. Each attempt carries a span link to the span that finished each of its dependencies. A duplicate served from an earlier result links to the span that produced that result.
- Attempts are deliberately not nested under their dependencies. A dependency's span has already ended when the dependent starts, and trace viewers treat that as clock skew. The project says Jaeger shifted such spans by up to 86ms and added warnings.
- A dead worker can't end its own span. The supervisor writes a `concord.attempt.lost` span for it, with `error.type` = `lease_expired`. A `concord.supervisor.requeue` child marks the requeue.
- Prompts and model outputs are never put on spans.
- The `gen_ai.*` attribute names follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions. The project says these are still in Development status and may need renames.
- The README says the planner, specialists and Claude client haven't been run against the real API yet. Tracing is measured against a mock model.

**Langfuse** [https://langfuse.com/docs/observability/data-model, https://langfuse.com/integrations/native/opentelemetry]
- A trace represents a single request or operation. It contains nested observations, and Langfuse calls OpenTelemetry spans observations.
- Observation types include span, generation and event. The OTel ingestion docs also accept agent, tool, chain, retriever, guardrail, evaluator and embedding through the `langfuse.observation.type` attribute.
- Trace-level attributes such as `user_id`, `session_id` and tags are carried on every observation. A session groups traces.
- A third-party article (not official docs) shows one trace per agent run, with nested spans per graph node and generations under them [https://medium.com/@_Ankit_Malviya/building-production-ready-langgraph-agents-with-langfuse-traces-prompt-registry-evals-and-c3f7cd903057].
- The Langfuse glossary also lists an "Agent Graph" view, which visualizes the flow of observations within a trace [https://langfuse.com/docs/glossary].

**Arize Phoenix** [https://arize.com/docs/phoenix/cookbook/tracing/openinference-best-practices]
- Phoenix uses the OpenInference conventions, which sit on top of OpenTelemetry spans.
- The `openinference.span.kind` attribute controls how Phoenix renders a span. The values are LLM, CHAIN, AGENT, TOOL, RETRIEVER, EMBEDDING, RERANKER, GUARDRAIL, EVALUATOR, PROMPT and UNKNOWN. Most applications use only LLM, chain, agent and tool.
- `session.id` groups multiple traces into a session.
- The page's example nests an outer agent workflow wrapper, an inner agent, chain spans per agent turn, and tool spans.

**Comparison**
- All three build on OpenTelemetry spans and trace IDs. Langfuse and Phoenix add their own attributes for typing spans (`langfuse.observation.type`, `openinference.span.kind`) and for grouping traces into sessions.
- Concord uses the standard `gen_ai.*` conventions plus its own `concord.*` attributes. The Langfuse ingestion docs say it also reads `gen_ai.request.model` [https://langfuse.com/integrations/native/opentelemetry], so Concord's `chat` spans may map onto Langfuse generations. I didn't verify that end to end.
- I found no Langfuse or Phoenix documentation on span links for dependencies, or on a lost-attempt equivalent. I didn't check whether either one uses span links, so I can't say whether they do.

ecf4a9750a5b63be70eff1746e3b74882e3e64ed.prompt_preview: Original question: How does Concord decide that two subgoals are duplicates, and how does that differ from how semantic
ecf4a9750a5b63be70eff1746e3b74882e3e64ed.text:
**Short answer:** Concord treats two subgoals as duplicates in two ways. One is an exact match on normalized text plus identical inputs. The other is embedding similarity above a threshold, which is off unless an embedder is supplied. Semantic caches like GPTCache decide two prompts are the same by embedding the prompt and accepting a nearby stored vector within a configurable threshold. The Concord side is well documented. The GPTCache side is only partly verified, as noted at the end.

**How Concord decides**
- The supervisor checks each subgoal before dispatch and reuses the earlier duplicate's output. A duplicate is defined as "same normalized text and same inputs, or embedding similarity above a threshold" [README.md § What works today].
- The two-part design exists because repeated subgoals usually arrive reworded [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions].
- Inputs are part of the comparison: "the same instruction applied to different inputs is different work" [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions].
- Similarity matching is off unless an embedder is supplied [README.md § Scorecard]. The shipped embedder is a word-overlap one meant for tests. It catches reordered or lightly edited subgoals but not true paraphrases, which need a real embedding model planned for a later phase [README.md § What works today].
- The threshold is mentioned but no value is given [README.md § What works today].
- The check happens in the lifecycle `pending → checking → ready → leased → done`, so a duplicate is caught before any worker spends tokens [ROADMAP.md § Design decisions]. The check span records an outcome of `dispatch`, `reuse` or `hold`, plus `concord.check.duplicate_of` and a reason [tracing.md § Span reference].
- Measured on 72 scripted runs with a mock model [README.md § Scorecard]:
  - Exact duplicates were caught 8/8, with 11.2% tokens saved.
  - Reworded duplicates were caught 0/16, because similarity was off.
  - There were 0/16 false alarms on healthy runs.
  - With the word-overlap embedder on, light edits were caught 7/8 in the harness and 38/40 in a larger run. True paraphrases were caught 0/40.
  - It reused the wrong output once in 40 look-alike runs, where subgoals differed only in topic.

**How GPTCache and similar semantic caches decide**
- GPTCache is an open-source semantic cache for LLM responses. Unlike exact-key caches such as Redis, it works through embeddings. It turns queries into vectors and runs similarity search in a vector store such as Milvus (https://aclanthology.org/2023.nlposs-1.24.pdf).
- Its components include an adapter, pre-processor, embedding generator and vector storage, and users can customize the embedding and other choices (https://aclanthology.org/2023.nlposs-1.24.pdf). A cache manager and similarity evaluator are also part of the paper's design, but that comes from the researcher's memory, not the text seen.
- For the generic mechanism, the closest verified evidence comes from LangChain's Redis caches, not GPTCache itself:
  - A query is embedded and the nearest stored embedding is accepted if it is within a distance threshold. A hit returns the cached response. A miss calls the LLM and caches the result (https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-17-how-to-implement-semantic-caching-with-langchain-and-memorystore-for-redis-on-gcp/view).
  - `RedisSemanticCache` uses `distance_threshold`, defaulting to 0.2, as "the maximum distance for considering a cache hit". Lowering it raises precision but may reduce hits (https://reference.langchain.com/python/langchain-redis/cache/RedisSemanticCache).
  - The older version keyed lookups on both the prompt and the LLM configuration string (https://sj-langchain.readthedocs.io/en/latest/cache/langchain.cache.RedisSemanticCache.html).
  - The threshold is described as the most important parameter to tune, and one user found good values needed experimentation (https://github.com/Redislabs-Solution-Architects/Redis-Workshops/issues/10).

**Direct comparison**

| Aspect | Concord | Semantic caches (GPTCache and similar) |
|---|---|---|
| What is compared | Subgoal text together with its inputs | The prompt, via its embedding. LangChain's Redis cache also keys on the LLM configuration string |
| Method | Exact match on normalized text and inputs, plus optional embedding similarity | Embedding similarity search over stored vectors |
| Threshold | Exists for the similarity path, value unstated. Similarity is off by default | Configurable distance cutoff. LangChain Redis defaults to 0.2. GPTCache's defaults were not established |
| Exact path | Yes, a first-class rule | Described as the alternative they replace. The Redis managed-service variant has an `use_exact_search` option, enabled by default (https://reference.langchain.com/python/langchain-redis/cache/LangCacheSemanticCache) |
| Purpose of a match | Avoid redundant work inside a multi-step plan by reusing an earlier subgoal's output before dispatch | Skip an LLM call by returning a stored response |
| Consequence | `reuse` or `hold`, logged with its reason. The duplicate never reaches a worker | Cached response returned. A miss calls the LLM and stores the result |

The main difference is that Concord makes the exact rule primary and requires identical inputs. Semantic caches rely on approximate vector distance. Both accept the same risk: a loose similarity match can return the wrong output, as Concord's one wrong reuse in 40 look-alike runs showed.

**Gaps**
- GPTCache's evaluator classes, default thresholds and how it picks a hit were not verified. The search tool hit its usage limit. The threshold figures above are from LangChain's Redis caches, not GPTCache.
- Concord's threshold value and text normalization are not documented in the passages. They also do not say whether the specialist or dependency list is compared, how a `hold` is resolved, or whether dependents are rewired.

ef9daea58e6ad02870e22d6058cdca26eb0e98e2.prompt_preview: Original question: How does Concord model a multi-agent run as an OpenTelemetry trace, and how do Langfuse and Arize Pho
ef9daea58e6ad02870e22d6058cdca26eb0e98e2.text:
Report on how Concord models a multi-agent run as an OpenTelemetry trace (from the passages only).

**Trace and root span**
- One run is one OpenTelemetry trace, with spans for the run, each pre-dispatch check, each attempt, model and tool calls, and blackboard writes, named after the GenAI semantic conventions. [README.md § What works today]
- The root span for the whole run is `invoke_workflow research-question` (1.55s in the example). [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]
- If the caller opens no root span, attempts hang off the short `concord.blackboard.submit` span and Jaeger reports clock-skew adjustments. The docs say to open a `workflow_span`. [tracing.md § Limits]

**Spans and parent/child structure**
- `concord.supervisor.check` spans are the pre-dispatch checks. Each has a `concord.blackboard.dispatch` child, the write that put the subgoal in the worker queue. [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]
- `invoke_agent specialist` spans are attempts. In the example, the search attempts each contain an `execute_tool web_search` call, a `chat mock-1` model call and a `concord.blackboard.complete` write nested inside. [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]
- Every attempt is a direct child of the run's root span. [tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgoal graph]
- Attempts are deliberately not nested under their dependencies. A dependency's span has already ended when the dependent starts, and trace viewers treat a child starting after its parent ended as clock skew. Jaeger shifted such spans by up to 86ms and attached warnings when an earlier version nested them. [tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgoal graph]
- Dependencies are expressed with span links instead: each attempt carries a span link to the span that finished each of its dependencies. A duplicate that the supervisor served from an earlier result links to the span that produced that result. [tracing.md § How the trace follows the subgoal graph]

**Supervisor, failures and retries**
- The supervisor appears as `concord.supervisor.check` spans (see above). [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]
- A lost attempt is `concord.attempt.lost` (shown red, about 1.05s each in the example). A dead worker cannot end its own span, so the supervisor writes this span on its behalf, covering the time the lease was held. Its child `concord.supervisor.requeue` marks when the supervisor put the subgoal back in the queue. [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]
- Retries by surviving workers appear as further `invoke_agent specialist` spans. [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]
- A worker process that really dies leaves no span of its own, which is why `concord.attempt.lost` exists. The two very short `invoke_agent` spans after the lost attempts in the example are an artifact of simulating a crash by cancelling the worker task. [tracing.md § What a trace looks like]

**Limits**
- Polling operations (lease attempts, heartbeats, the supervisor's periodic reclaim) are not traced. [tracing.md § Limits]
- No tools exist yet, so `execute_tool` spans only appear in the example and tests. [tracing.md § Limits]

**Not covered by the passages**
- The passages do not list span attributes (for example specific `gen_ai.*` or `concord.*` attribute keys). They say only that spans are named after the GenAI semantic conventions.
- They do not describe how individual sub-agents are distinguished beyond the span name `invoke_agent specialist`.
- They say nothing about Langfuse or Arize Phoenix.

f4402017905a9b385c6f2b6e3159706d6b06efcb.prompt_preview: Original question: How do Temporal, Celery and AWS Step Functions each detect a worker that dies in the middle of a task
f4402017905a9b385c6f2b6e3159706d6b06efcb.text:
**Short answer:** Temporal and Celery are covered below from sourced findings. Step Functions could not be verified, so its section is mostly a statement of what is missing.

- **Temporal** does not detect a crash directly. It relies on timeouts (Start-To-Close, optionally Heartbeat) and then retries the activity on another worker.
- **Celery** has no built-in mid-task crash detection for the task itself. What happens depends on when the message is acknowledged, and recovery is broker redelivery.
- **AWS Step Functions** could not be answered from verified sources (see below).

## Temporal

**Detection**
- The server does not detect a worker crash or lost communication directly. It relies on the Start-To-Close Timeout to force Activity retries. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- Start-To-Close has no default. If only Schedule-To-Close is set, that value is used. If neither is set, the service rejects the activity. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- Heartbeats are optional pings from the worker to the service. If none arrive within the Heartbeat Timeout, the activity is considered failed. https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection
- Heartbeats detect a crash faster than waiting for Start-To-Close, and the docs recommend them for long-running activities. https://docs.temporal.io/design-patterns/long-running-activity, https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- Schedule-To-Start is mainly for detecting that the worker fleet is not keeping up, not a single crash. Its default is infinity. https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures
- Workflow tasks have their own timeout. https://docs.temporal.io/references/events

**Recovery**
- On a timeout, the server records an ActivityTaskTimedOut event and retries according to the RetryPolicy. It puts the task back on the Activity Task Queue and increments the attempt count. https://temporal.io/blog/activity-timeouts
- Any available worker can pick it up. After a crash and heartbeat timeout, the Activity is retried on a new Worker, which can read the last heartbeat details and resume from a checkpoint. https://docs.temporal.io/design-patterns/long-running-activity
- With no custom retry policy, a default one retries until a timeout threshold is reached. https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection The blog says retries can continue for up to 10 years with backoff. https://temporal.io/blog/activity-timeouts
- If the retry policy allows only one attempt, the activity is not retried. https://docs.temporal.io/activity-execution
- For workflow tasks, the worker drops its cached state after a failure or timeout. The next task is polled from the regular queue and the workflow history is replayed. https://community.temporal.io/t/handling-workflow-task-timeout-due-to-sticky-queue-task-timeout/16443 A sticky queue's schedule-to-start timeout lets a task fall back to the regular queue if its sticky worker is gone. https://github.com/temporalio/sdk-rust/blob/main/arch_docs/sticky_queues.md

**Gaps:** I found no official page confirming the default workflow task timeout, the default sticky schedule-to-start timeout, or the default retry policy values.

## Celery

**Detection and recovery depend on acknowledgement**
- **Default (early ack):** the worker acknowledges the message just before running the task, so a started task is never executed again. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html The sources do not say outright that the task is lost if the worker dies mid-run. That is my inference, since the message is already acknowledged.
- **`acks_late` (off by default):** the message is acknowledged after execution. The task may run twice or more if the worker crashes mid-execution. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html, https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/reference/celery.app.task.html
- **Pool child killed:** even with `acks_late`, the worker acknowledges the task if the executing process exits abruptly or is signaled. Setting `task_reject_on_worker_lost` requeues it instead, so it runs again on the same or another worker. It is off by default, and the docs warn it can cause message loops. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html
- `worker_lost_wait` (default 10 seconds) controls how long Celery waits for missing results before raising a worker-lost error. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html A user report says `AsyncResult.get()` raised `WorkerLostError` even after the task was rescheduled. That report is internally inconsistent, so treat it as unconfirmed. https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/4229
- **Broker-side redelivery (Redis and similar):** the visibility timeout is how long the broker waits for an ack before redelivering to another worker. The Redis default is 1 hour. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/getting-started/backends-and-brokers/redis.html Unacked messages are also redelivered when the connection closes. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v5.5.1/history/whatsnew-3.0.html
- **Worker heartbeats:** workers send `worker-heartbeat` events every 2 seconds by default. https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/internals/reference/celery.worker.heartbeat.html These are distinct from AMQP protocol-level heartbeats. https://celery-safwan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/celery.worker.consumer.html I could not confirm that they are monitoring-only, or how long a monitor waits before treating a worker as offline.

**Gaps:** I did not confirm how the main process notices a dead pool child, or the exact `WorkerLostError` text.

## AWS Step Functions

I could not verify any of this. The research hit a tool limit before any content was read, so I make no claims about how Step Functions detects a dead worker or recovers. Unverified topics:
- how `TimeoutSeconds` and `HeartbeatSeconds` work, and when `States.Timeout` and `States.HeartbeatTimeout` are raised
- `Retry` and `Catch` configuration
- redrive of failed executions
- activity task token handling (`GetActivityTask`, `SendTaskHeartbeat`, and so on)

Pages that would answer this are the Step Functions Developer Guide pages on error handling, activities (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-activities.html), and redriving executions. A glimpsed boto3 snippet (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/boto3/latest/reference/services/stepfunctions/client/send_task_heartbeat.html) only mentions the task's Timeout in the state machine definition. A secondary blog (https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-30-aws-step-functions-best-practices/view) says `States.Timeout` means the task exceeded `TimeoutSeconds`. Neither is enough to rely on.

## Comparison

- **Default behavior:** Temporal retries by default, with a default retry policy, once a timeout fires. Celery's default (early ack) does not redeliver a task whose worker died. Step Functions is unverified.
- **Who owns the state:** Temporal's server holds the workflow history and activity attempt state, so recovery needs nothing from the dead worker. Celery leaves it to the broker's acknowledgement and redelivery, which differ by broker. Step Functions is unverified.
- **What the user must configure:** Temporal needs a Start-To-Close or Schedule-To-Close timeout (otherwise the activity is rejected), and ideally heartbeats for long activities. Celery needs `acks_late`, optionally `reject_on_worker_lost`, idempotent tasks, and a suitable visibility timeout. Step Functions is unverified.

f4d22fcf3e6e739d7cd9fee8ecea585d6b2b20b1.prompt_preview: Question: What mechanisms do the Claude API, the OpenAI API and LangGraph provide for capping the tokens or steps an age
f4d22fcf3e6e739d7cd9fee8ecea585d6b2b20b1.text:
Short answer: I could confirm the Claude and OpenAI mechanisms, but not LangGraph's. My search quota ran out before I could reach LangGraph's documentation. I'm not filling that gap from memory.

**Claude API**
- Task budgets give Claude an advisory token budget for the whole agentic loop (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/task-budgets).
- The page says Claude may exceed the budget if it is mid-action and stopping would be more disruptive than finishing (same URL).
- The enforced limit on total output tokens is still `max_tokens`, which truncates the response (same URL).
- So the budget is a soft cap and `max_tokens` is the hard one. The page does not mention a step or turn cap, and I did not find one. Any loop-level cap on the Claude API would have to be one you write yourself.
- I only saw a snippet of this page, so check it for details such as which models support task budgets.

**OpenAI**
- The Agents SDK has a step cap, `max_turns`, on `Runner.run`, `run_sync` and `run_streamed`.
  - A turn is one LLM call in the agent loop (https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/).
  - Going over the limit raises `MaxTurnsExceeded`. Passing `max_turns=None` disables the limit (same URL).
  - You can pass `error_handlers={"max_turns": ...}` to return a fallback final output instead of an exception (same URL).
  - The `Runner.run` reference shows `max_turns` defaulting to `DEFAULT_MAX_TURNS` (https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ref/run/).
- I did not retrieve documentation for OpenAI's plain API token parameters, such as `max_output_tokens` or `max_tool_calls`. I can't confirm them here.

**LangGraph**
- Not found. I can't say what it provides without a source.
- A search on `recursion_limit` and `GraphRecursionError` in LangGraph's docs would be the place to start.

**Concord's own supervisor**
- The README says the supervisor halts the run when it goes over its token budget. Your own code therefore already does what the Claude advisory budget cannot, which is stop the run (README.md § What works today).

fa6515a80e4e8cb1a01e885241308c3aef5b625b.prompt_preview: Original question: How does Jaeger's clock skew adjustment work, when does it change span timestamps, and how can it be
fa6515a80e4e8cb1a01e885241308c3aef5b625b.text:
Need algorithm details; search source.Get the rest of the source.I could confirm the conditions, the config switch and where the adjustment runs. I could not get the full algorithm source, so the shift formula is only partly confirmed.

**Where and when it runs**
- The adjustment runs in the query service, not at storage time. The query service applies it before returning data to API clients: "StandardAdjusters is a list of model adjusters applied by the query service before returning the data to the API clients." https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/cmd/query/app/querysvc
- `ClockSkew` is one of the standard adjusters. In v1.x the list was SpanIDDeduper, ClockSkew, IPTagAdjuster, SortLogFields and SpanReferences. https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/thinkerou/jaeger/cmd/query/app/querysvc
- The newer v2 query service builds its list with `StandardAdjusters(maxClockSkewAdjust)`. https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/cmd/query/app/querysvc/v2/adjuster
- The docs say the setting applies to all traces retrieved from the given query service. https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/
- Because the adjustment happens on read, I infer that stored data is not rewritten. I did not find a source that says this outright.

**Which spans are shifted**
- The source comment says the adjuster modifies start time and log timestamps of spans that look "off" relative to the parent because of clock skew on different servers. The main condition is that child spans must not start before or end after their parent spans. https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.67.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- The adjuster works on a tree of spans built from parent references (it builds a node map and sub-graphs, then adjusts from each root). The same file shows this. https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.67.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- It assumes span IDs are unique, so it runs after the span-ID de-duplication step. https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.67.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- Spans from different hosts only:
  - In v2, a host key is derived from resource attributes such as `host.id`, `host.ip` or `host.name`. Spans with the same host key are treated as the same source, and no skew adjustment is expected between them. https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/cmd/query/app/querysvc/v2/adjuster
  - In v1, issue #1459 says the host was identified by the process `ip` tag, and that a missing tag was treated as a different host. https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/1459 This is a user's description, not documentation.
- If a child already fits inside its parent, no adjustment is made. The snippet reads "child already fits within the parent span, do not adjust" and returns 0. https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.59.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go

**How the shift is computed (partial)**
- The code comment says network latency is assumed to be split equally between request and response. https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.59.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- The docs describe the effect: the child span is repositioned within its parent, placed in the middle of the parent span. Jaeger does not know the real request/response latency split. https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/
- Issue #1459 criticizes the algorithm's duration comparisons and its assumption that span duration correlates with network latency. https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/issues/1459
- I did not retrieve the exact formula. Likely it is the parent duration minus the child duration, halved, but that is not confirmed.

**Logs and descendants**
- Log timestamps are shifted along with start times. This is confirmed by the source comment and the v2 docs ("start and log timestamps"). https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/cmd/query/app/querysvc/v2/adjuster
- The code carries a `skew` value down from each root (`adjustNode(n, nil, skew)`), which suggests descendants inherit the parent's adjustment. I could not see the body of `adjustNode`, so this is not confirmed.

**Limits, warnings and failures**
- A maximum delta (`maxDelta`) caps the adjustment. If the calculated delta exceeds it, the span is not shifted. A warning is recorded: "max clock skew adjustment delta of %v exceeded; not applying calculated delta of %v". https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.67.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- When adjustment is disabled, the code uses the warning "clock skew adjustment disabled; not applying calculated delta of %v". Other warnings cover duplicate span IDs and invalid parent IDs; both skip the adjustment. https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.67.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- The adjuster never returns errors. It records problems in `Span.Warnings`. https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger/blob/v1.59.0/model/adjuster/clockskew.go
- Adjusted spans show a UI warning giving the exact skew delta applied. https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/2.22/deployment/configuration/

**Turning it off**
- In Jaeger v2, set `max_clock_skew_adjust` to `0s` on the `jaeger_query` extension. https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/2.22/deployment/configuration/
- In v1, use the flag `--query.max-clock-skew-adjustment=0s`. https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/1.20/deployment/
- This is a server-wide setting. A UI toggle is still an open ticket (#197). https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/2.22/deployment/configuration/
- A third-party blog mentions the environment variable `QUERY_MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_ADJUSTMENT`. I did not verify it against Jaeger docs. https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-06-resolve-clock-skew-opentelemetry-distributed-traces/view

**Not established**
- The exact shift formula.
- Whether descendants are shifted by the inherited delta.
- What happens in the v2 code when a span's host key is missing.

fbe293f5c203dc7dd2c11fc95205b699d4c27c1d.text:

**What I found:**
- The `Runner.run` reference page says the agent may raise an exception in two cases. First, if `max_turns` is exceeded, a `MaxTurnsExceeded` exception is raised "unless handled". Second, if a guardrail tripwire is triggered, the matching tripwire exception is raised, for example `InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered`. Source: https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ref/run/
- I saw only the snippet that opens that page, not the full page. Its mention of "unless handled" hints at an error-handler mechanism for max turns, but I did not confirm how it works.

**What I could not establish.** I did not verify any of the following from sources, and I am not filling them in from memory:
- Model or API retry settings. This covers whether the SDK has a retry configuration in `ModelSettings`, and how the underlying OpenAI client's default retries behave.
- Timeouts. I did not confirm per-model-call timeouts or per-tool timeouts.
- Tool failure handling. I did not confirm `failure_error_function` or how tool errors are returned to the model.
- Sessions. I did not confirm session persistence (SQLiteSession, Redis and similar) or what it saves.
- Run state and resumption. I did not confirm `RunState` serialization or resuming after human-in-the-loop approvals.
- Durable execution. I did not confirm the Temporal, DBOS or Restate integrations.
- Checkpointing. I did not confirm whether the SDK has built-in, LangGraph-style checkpointing.

The writer should treat all of these as unverified. The places to check are the official docs at openai.github.io/openai-agents-python (pages for running agents, sessions, guardrails, tools, human-in-the-loop and the exceptions reference) and the Temporal and OpenAI integration documentation.

ff047d20d9a9d8f85394cf6c3ba6f7b516757e73.prompt_preview: Original question: What span names and attributes do the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define for agent invoc
ff047d20d9a9d8f85394cf6c3ba6f7b516757e73.text:
Results are a JSON string.I could not confirm everything against primary documents, because the search tool hit its usage limit. Several points below rest on secondary sources. The primary pages I did get are the release notes for semantic-conventions v1.38.0 and the releases list, plus the agent-spans page in the new repository.

**Stability status**
- The agent-spans document in the new GenAI repository marks the "Invoke agent client span" as **Status: Development**. Source: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md
- I did not open the other documents there (model spans, metrics, events, exceptions, MCP), so I have not confirmed their status first-hand. A secondary source says every document in the repository is still in Development, so attribute names can change between releases. Source: https://www.matthewswong.com/en/blog/opentelemetry-genai-agent-spans-tracing/
- Other secondary sources agree that GenAI is not stable.
  - One says the spec is still in Development. Source: https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions
  - Another, written as of April 2026, says the `gen_ai.*` namespace was experimental or in development at v1.40.0 (February 2026). Source: https://dev.to/gabrielanhaia/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-your-llm-traces-should-look-like-this-in-2026-3ff6
  - A third is titled to say the conventions are not stable yet. Source: https://dev.to/azena-ai/opentelemetrys-genai-semantic-conventions-are-not-stable-yet-heres-what-actually-shipped-in-2026-3mke
- Older docs also labelled these conventions "Experimental". Source (v1.27.0 era): https://hexdocs.pm/opentelemetry_semantic_conventions/1.27.0/readme-24.html

**Repository move (a recent structural change)**
- The main semantic-conventions releases page lists a breaking change: the Generative AI conventions moved to a dedicated repository (#3696). All `gen_ai.*` attributes, metrics, events and spans that were under `model/gen-ai/`, `model/openai/` and `model/mcp/` moved. Source: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/releases
- The new repository is `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai`, with documents under `docs/gen-ai/`. The files named are `gen-ai-spans.md`, `gen-ai-agent-spans.md`, `gen-ai-metrics.md`, `gen-ai-events.md`, `gen-ai-exceptions.md` and `mcp.md`. Source: https://hidekazu-konishi.com/entry/opentelemetry_genai_semantic_conventions_guide.html
- Secondary sources say the old opentelemetry.io `semconv/gen-ai` pages are now redirect stubs or point to the new repository with a "no longer maintained" notice. Sources: https://www.dash0.com/knowledge/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained and the matthewswong.com link above.
- One article dates the move to June 2026. Source: https://www.truefoundry.com/blog/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions
- The same hidekazu-konishi guide says the new repository has no tagged releases and its changelog has only an "Unreleased" section. So there is no GenAI-specific version number to cite. That claim comes from a secondary source and I did not check it against the repository.

**Opt-in mechanism: `OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN`**
- Setting `OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=gen_ai_latest_experimental` makes instrumentation emit the latest experimental GenAI conventions. Without it, instrumentation that predates v1.37 keeps emitting the older format by default.
  - Datadog describes it as enabling v1.37+-compliant traces for frameworks that previously supported older versions, such as strands-agents. Source: https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/instrumentation/otel_instrumentation/
  - Greptime describes v1.36 as the transition baseline, with existing instrumentations defaulting to the old format. Source: https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions
- I did not retrieve the official text defining this variable's other values, such as a `gen_ai_latest_experimental` versus a dual-emit option. I can't say whether others exist.

**Version history and renames (from secondary sources)**
- **v1.37:** the chat history handling was revamped. `gen_ai.system` was replaced by `gen_ai.provider.name`. Source: https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions
- **v1.38.0:** tool definitions and execution details were added for single- and multi-agent systems, including a `gen_ai.tool.definitions` attribute on the `invoke_agent` span. This is from the primary release notes: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/releases/tag/v1.38.0
- **v1.38.0, deprecations:** an issue in the traceloop/openllmetry repository says `gen_ai.prompt` and `gen_ai.completion` are deprecated and removed from the spec as of v1.38.0. Source: https://github.com/traceloop/openllmetry/issues/3515
- **Other renames:** `gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens` became `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, with a matching change for completion tokens (the source snippet was cut off). Source: https://dev.to/azena-ai/opentelemetrys-genai-semantic-conventions-are-not-stable-yet-heres-what-actually-shipped-in-2026-3mke
- **`gen_ai.provider.name`:** a secondary source says it was removed as a required attribute. Source: https://hidekazu-konishi.com/entry/opentelemetry_genai_semantic_conventions_guide.html
- Greptime's table says every release up to v1.41 included GenAI changes. Source: https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions

**Version checked and gaps**
- The newest core semantic-conventions version I saw referenced is v1.41 (Greptime). I confirmed v1.38.0 directly.
- I could not confirm the exact latest core version, or the exact commit or date of the new GenAI repository, from a primary source.
- I did not verify the full per-version rename list against the official registry deprecation pages.

ff65584064f831e362e7e72578028b394d243d6a.prompt_preview: Original question: What mechanisms do the Claude API, the OpenAI API and LangGraph provide for capping the tokens or ste
ff65584064f831e362e7e72578028b394d243d6a.text:
**Short answer:** Only the Claude API side is documented in what I was given. The OpenAI and LangGraph research did not complete (searches failed), so I can't confirm those mechanisms. I have not filled the gap from memory.

## Claude API

**Token caps**
- **`max_tokens` (per request):** Required on Messages API calls. It is an absolute maximum on generated tokens, and the model may stop earlier. When it is hit, `stop_reason` is `max_tokens` (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons). The parameter description comes from a third-party compatibility page, not Anthropic's own docs (https://mimo.mi.com/docs/en-US/api/chat/anthropic-api). It caps one request only, not a cumulative budget across an agent loop. That last point is an inference, not something the sources state.
- **Extended thinking `budget_tokens`:** Sets a target for reasoning tokens. The minimum is 1,024, and it must be less than `max_tokens`, because thinking counts toward that limit. With interleaved thinking it can exceed `max_tokens`, since the budget spans all thinking blocks in a turn. The docs call it a target, not a strict cap (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking). LangChain notes Opus 4.6+ can use adaptive thinking, which sets the budget automatically (https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/chat/anthropic).

**Step caps**
- **`max_uses` on the web search tool:** Limits searches per request. The docs describe it as a hard constraint. Exceeding it returns a `web_search_tool_result` error with code `max_uses_exceeded` (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/web-search-tool). I did not check whether other server tools have an equivalent.
- **SDK tool runner `max_iterations`:** `client.beta.messages.tool_runner(...)` loops until Claude returns no tool use, or until `max_iterations` if set. You can also `break` out of the loop (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-runner). The limit is optional with no apparent default. I only saw Python examples, so availability in other SDKs is unconfirmed.

**Gap:** I found no API-level cap on cumulative tokens or turns in a hand-written tool-use loop. There, your own code must count iterations and usage. This is absence of evidence, not a documented statement. I also couldn't find the full text of the `pause_turn` stop reason.

## OpenAI API

Unverified. The research retrieved no confirmed findings. Candidates to check against OpenAI's documentation are:
- `max_output_tokens` (Responses API)
- `max_completion_tokens` (Chat Completions)
- `max_tool_calls` (Responses API)
- reasoning effort controls
- `max_turns` in the Agents SDK `Runner`

Pages worth consulting include https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning and https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/, but I have no confirmed content from them.

## LangGraph

Largely unverified. The only retrieved item is a GitHub bug report, not official documentation, saying a graph that finishes on the last step `recursion_limit` allows still raises `GraphRecursionError` even though every node has run (https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/issues/9163). That suggests a `recursion_limit` step cap exists, but I could not confirm where it is set, its default, or details such as `RemainingSteps`, `create_react_agent` behavior, `trim_messages` token trimming, or model-call-limit middleware. Official pointers: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/errors/GRAPH_RECURSION_LIMIT and https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/errors/GraphRecursionError.

## Comparison

| | Token cap | Step cap |
|---|---|---|
| Claude API | `max_tokens` per request; `budget_tokens` is a target for thinking | `max_uses` for web search; optional `max_iterations` in the SDK tool runner |
| OpenAI API | Unverified | Unverified |
| LangGraph | Unverified | Probably `recursion_limit` (single bug report only) |

For Claude, the confirmed caps are per request or per tool, and there is no built-in cumulative token budget for an agent run. A like-for-like comparison across the three platforms isn't possible until the OpenAI and LangGraph documentation is checked.

ffe5958c23b2374f5fcfc1c2efa33fbb5fc27b01.prompt_preview: Original question: According to the MAST taxonomy from the paper 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?', what are the th
ffe5958c23b2374f5fcfc1c2efa33fbb5fc27b01.text:
**The three MAST failure categories** (Cemri et al., "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?", arXiv 2503.13657; https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657). MAST has 14 failure modes grouped into three categories:

1. **System design issues** (FC1, also called "specification issues" in later papers)
2. **Inter-agent misalignment** (FC2)
3. **Task verification** (FC3)

**Most common individual failure modes.** The per-mode figures below come from Figure 1 of arXiv v3 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13657), which reports prevalence across 1,642 traces. Most of the mode-to-number mapping was reconstructed from scrambled PDF text, so treat the individual values as likely but not directly confirmed.
1. Step Repetition (1.3): 15.7%
2. Reasoning-Action Mismatch (2.6): 13.2%. A dev.to field guide independently gives the same figure (https://dev.to/tuomo_pisama/a-field-guide-to-multi-agent-failure-modes-59on).
3. Unaware of Termination Conditions (1.5): 12.4%
4. Disobey Task Specification (1.1): 11.8%
5. Incorrect Verification (3.3): 9.1% (inferred)
6. No or Incomplete Verification (3.2): 8.2% (inferred). A secondary blog gives the same 9.1% and 8.2% for these two modes (https://futureagi.substack.com/p/why-do-multi-agent-llm-systems-fail).

Other modes are much rarer. Task Derailment (2.3) is 7.40% and Information Withholding (2.4) is 0.80%, both explicitly confirmed. Conversation Reset (2.1) is 2.20% and Fail to Ask for Clarification (2.2) is 6.80%, also confirmed in the extracted text. I found no prose in the paper that explicitly ranks the modes. The ranking is derived from the figure values.

**Modes by category**
- FC1: Disobey Task Specification (1.1), Disobey Role Specification (1.2), Step Repetition (1.3), Loss of Conversation History (1.4), Unaware of Termination Conditions (1.5). Modes 1.2 and 1.5 were not seen in the NeurIPS text and were filled in from memory. A separate paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.17915) lists all five, which supports this.
- FC2: Conversation Reset, Fail to Ask for Clarification, Task Derailment, Information Withholding, Ignored Other Agent's Input, Reasoning-Action Mismatch (2.1–2.6).
- FC3: Premature Termination, No or Incomplete Verification, Incorrect Verification (3.1–3.3).

**Discrepancies between sources**
- **Category shares differ by version.** arXiv v3 Figure 1 gives system design 44.2%, inter-agent misalignment 32.3% and task verification 23.5%. The NeurIPS version gives 41.8%, 36.9% and 21.3% on MAST-Data (210 traces) (https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/b1041e52d3be19f0a9bc491657488e4a-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf). A later paper (arXiv 2606.08162) reports the NeurIPS-style 41.77%, 36.94% and 21.30%. In both versions system design is the largest category and task verification the smallest.
- **Earlier versions had different numbers.** The arXiv PDF text also contains values such as 37.17% for Step Repetition and 7.59% for Reasoning-Action Mismatch. I couldn't tell which version they come from, so cite v3 or the NeurIPS version.
- **Trace counts vary.** The abstract says the taxonomy was developed from 150 traces (inter-annotator kappa = 0.88). The NeurIPS figure uses 210 traces, and arXiv v3 and secondary sources cite about 1,600 or more. These probably refer to different stages of the work, but I did not confirm that.
